short_definition: Passive or instructed viewing of emotionally valenced images (IAPS, GAPED, NAPS, OASIS) while physiological, neural, or rating responses to valence and arousal are recorded.
description: Participants passively view color photographs from the International Affective Picture System (IAPS), a validated database of 1,182 images varying in emotional valence (pleasant, unpleasant, neutral) and arousal (calm to exciting). Images are presented for 3-5 seconds each without requiring an overt response. Post-viewing, participants rate valence and arousal on 9-point scales. The task serves as a standardized emotion elicitation tool in neuroimaging, consistently activating amygdala (for high-arousal images), visual cortex (enhanced processing of emotional stimuli), and prefrontal regions.

procedure: Participants view emotionally valenced images (e.g., IAPS) presented for several seconds each.
Participants may rate valence and arousal or simply view while physiological signals are recorded.
manipulations: Emotional valence (positive, negative, neutral) and arousal level of the images
Picture selection (single discrete emotion per block vs. mixed valence and arousal)

material: Color photographs from a validated set such as the International Affective Picture System, varying in emotional valence (pleasant, unpleasant, neutral) and arousal.

variants.name: Category-Specific Selection
variants.note: Pictures are chosen to evoke one discrete emotion at a time and shown in blocks of a single emotion instead of a mixed valence-by-arousal set.

families.rationale: View valenced images

short_definition: Target evaluation (good/bad) preceded by a briefly presented affective prime; response facilitation on congruent trials indexes automatic evaluation.
description: Participants categorize target stimuli (e.g., judge words as "good" or "bad") that are immediately preceded by briefly presented prime stimuli (words, faces, or images) of matching or mismatching emotional valence. The affective priming effect (faster RT for congruent vs. incongruent prime-target pairs) reflects automatic activation of evaluative representations. Subliminal variants (very brief prime exposure) provide evidence for unconscious emotional processing.

procedure: A briefly presented prime (word, face, or image with positive or negative valence) is followed by a target that participants evaluate as good/bad or classify.
manipulations: Congruence between prime valence and target valence
Prime and target type (words, emotional pictures, emotional faces)
measurements: RT and accuracy for target evaluation
Congruency effect (faster on congruent trials) indexes automatic affective evaluation

material: A briefly shown prime (a word, face or image of positive or negative valence) followed by a target word to be judged good or bad.

variants.name: Pronunciation/Naming
variants.note: The participant reads the target word aloud instead of judging its valence, so the response names the word itself rather than its category.

variants.name: Picture-Word Priming
variants.note: The prime is an emotional photograph instead of a word; the target word is still judged good or bad.

variants.name: Face-Face Priming
variants.note: Both prime and target are emotional faces and the target's expression is classified (happy or angry) instead of a word being judged good or bad.

variants.name: Cross-Modal Affective Priming
variants.note: The prime is heard through headphones while the target is a written word; the judgment is unchanged.

families.rationale: Evaluative priming; the congruence structure could argue for conflict and interference

short_definition: Participants must suppress a prepotent saccade toward a peripheral cue and generate a voluntary saccade to the opposite location; errors and saccade latency index oculomotor inhibition.
description: The Anti-Saccade Task measures voluntary control over reflexive eye movements. Participants fixate centrally while a peripheral stimulus suddenly appears in the left or right visual field. Instead of looking toward the stimulus (the reflexive prosaccade), participants must look in the opposite direction (antisaccade). This requires inhibiting the automatic orienting response and generating a volitional saccade. Performance is measured by antisaccade accuracy, latency, and the rate of prosaccadic intrusions (errors). The task indexes voluntary oculomotor control and prefrontal inhibitory function.

procedure: A peripheral cue appears.
Participants must suppress the reflexive saccade toward it and instead generate a voluntary saccade to the mirror-opposite location.
manipulations: Prosaccade vs. antisaccade blocks or interleaved trials
Response release (delayed go signal vs. immediate)
Cue type (emotional face or picture vs. dot)
Memory delay before the saccade (memory-guided vs. visually guided)
Second cue or target jump during saccade planning (double step)
measurements: Saccade direction errors (% erroneous prosaccades on antisaccade trials)

material: A central fixation point and a stimulus that appears suddenly in the left or right periphery.

combined_with.note: Gaze is held on the fixation target until the peripheral target appears.

variants.name: Prosaccade (Control Condition)
variants.note: The same display but the participant looks toward the cue, so the opposite-response demand is dropped.

variants.name: Interleaved Pro/Anti-Saccade
variants.note: Look-toward and look-away trials are mixed in one block and a per-trial cue (often fixation color) says which rule applies.

variants.name: Blocked Pro/Anti-Saccade
variants.note: Prosaccade and antisaccade trials are run in separate blocks, so within each block the rule is fixed and the task alternates between the standard form and the prosaccade control.

variants.name: Emotional Anti-Saccade
variants.note: The peripheral cue is an emotional face or picture instead of a dot; the look-away rule is unchanged.

variants.name: Memory-Guided Anti-Saccade
variants.note: The cue disappears, its location is held in memory through a delay, and the look-away saccade is made to the remembered mirror location on a later signal.

variants.name: Double-Step Anti-Saccade
variants.note: A second cue arrives, or the target jumps, while the first saccade is being planned or executed, so the participant must re-program a response already under way.

families.rationale: Suppress the reflexive saccade and look away

short_definition: Exposure to letter strings generated by a finite-state grammar followed by a grammaticality judgment on novel strings; indexes implicit rule learning.
description: Participants are first exposed to letter strings (e.g., "MXRVXT," "VXTTRM") generated by a finite-state grammar, often under the cover story that they are memorizing the strings. In a subsequent test phase, they classify novel letter strings as grammatical or non-grammatical, performing above chance despite being unable to articulate the underlying rules. Reber (1967) introduced this paradigm as the first laboratory demonstration of implicit learning - the acquisition of complex, rule-governed knowledge without conscious awareness. The paradigm has been central to debates about the nature of implicit vs. explicit knowledge, the role of consciousness in learning, and the neural systems supporting rule abstraction.

procedure: Participants study letter strings generated by a finite-state grammar during a training phase, then classify novel strings as grammatical or not.
Optional: The test strings use a different letter set from training arranged by the same grammar, so only abstract rule knowledge can carry over.
manipulations: Surface features (same vs. changed letter set at test)
Presentation format (sequential, element by element vs. whole strings)

material: Letter strings (such as MXRVXT) generated by a finite-state grammar, and at test new strings that do or do not follow it.

variants.name: Production Task
variants.note: After training the participant writes or types new strings they believe follow the grammar, instead of judging whether given strings follow it.

variants.name: Sequential AGL
variants.note: Each string arrives one letter at a time at a set pace, and the participant may be asked to predict or respond to each next letter, so the task becomes learning what follows what.

variants.name: Cross-Modal AGL
variants.note: The strings are presented as sequences of sounds or touches instead of letters, or training is in one modality and test in another, with the same grammaticality judgment at test.

families.rationale: Implicit rule learning from exposure to strings

short_definition: Identify the direction of a central arrow flanked by congruent or incongruent arrows, preceded by various cue types; RT differences across cue and flanker conditions index three independent attention networks (alerting, orienting, executive).
description: The Attention Network Test (ANT) combines elements of the Posner cueing paradigm and the Eriksen flanker task to provide separate measures of three attention networks in a single task. Participants respond to the direction of a central arrow flanked by congruent or incongruent flankers, with the target preceded by no cue, a center cue, a double cue, or a spatial cue. The ANT yields three independent efficiency scores: alerting (double cue benefit over no cue), orienting (spatial cue benefit over center cue), and executive control (incongruent flanker cost). The task operationalizes Posner's attention network model.

procedure: Flanker task with preceding spatial and temporal cues.
Participants identify the direction of a central arrow flanked by congruent or incongruent arrows.
manipulations: Cue type (no cue, center cue, double cue, spatial cue)
Cue validity and cue-target interval (invalid spatial cues; varied interval)
Display position (lateralized left or right vs. above and below fixation)
Emotional stimuli as cues or flankers
measurements: Alerting network score (double-cue minus no-cue RT)
Orienting network score (center-cue minus spatial-cue RT)
Executive network score (incongruent minus congruent RT)

material: A central arrow between flanking arrows that point the same or the opposite way, preceded by no cue, a center cue, a double cue or a spatial cue.

combined_with.note: Gaze is held on the fixation target while the main game is played.

variants.name: ANT-I (Callejas et al.)
variants.note: The alerting cue becomes a tone and the location cue a separate visual cue, varied independently on every trial so the network effects can interact; the cue types are the same as the standard, only factorially crossed and partly auditory.

variants.name: Child ANT
variants.note: Cartoon fish replace the arrows, trials are slower, feedback is given and the task is framed as feeding the fish.

variants.name: ANT with Emotional Stimuli
variants.note: Emotional pictures or faces serve as cues or replace the neutral flankers; the task is unchanged.

families.rationale: Cueing combined with a flanker; filed by its cue manipulation

short_definition: Detect, discriminate, or identify a target sound in the presence of a masking sound; threshold shifts between masked and unmasked conditions index frequency selectivity, temporal resolution, and auditory scene analysis.
description: A target sound (tone, speech token, or noise burst) is presented alongside, before, or after a masking sound, and participants detect, discriminate, or identify the target. By varying the temporal and spectral relationship between target and masker, the paradigm dissociates peripheral (energetic) masking - where masker and target excite overlapping auditory filters - from central (informational) masking - where the masker is spectrally remote but introduces perceptual uncertainty. Threshold shifts, psychometric functions, and comodulation masking release are the core dependent measures. The paradigm is foundational to auditory psychophysics and clinical audiology, and maps onto distinct subcortical and cortical processing stages.

procedure: A target sound is presented alongside, before, or after a masker.
Participants detect, discriminate, or identify the target.
manipulations: Spectral overlap between target and masker

material: A target sound (a tone, a speech token or a noise burst) presented with, before or after a masker of noise, tones, speech or modulated sound.

variants.name: Speech-in-noise
variants.note: The target is spoken words or sentences and the participant repeats or identifies what was said rather than reporting presence.

variants.name: Spatial release from masking
variants.note: Target and masker are played from different directions and the threshold is compared with the co-located case.

families.rationale: Detection or discrimination of a sound in noise

short_definition: Sequential pumping of a virtual balloon for monetary reward with stochastic popping; average pumps per un-popped balloon indexes risk-taking.
description: Participants inflate a virtual balloon by clicking a pump button, earning money with each pump. The balloon may explode at any point, causing loss of all accumulated earnings for that trial. Participants can cash out at any time to save their earnings. The average number of pumps before cashing out indexes risk-taking propensity. BART risk-taking correlates with real-world risky behaviors. fMRI reveals activation in ventromedial PFC, anterior insula, and striatal regions during risk assessment.

procedure: Participants sequentially pump a virtual balloon for incremental monetary reward.
Each pump risks the balloon popping and losing that trial's earnings.
They can stop and bank at any time.
manipulations: Pump decision (committed in advance vs. during inflation)
measurements: Adjusted average pumps on un-popped balloons (risk-taking index)

material: A virtual balloon that grows with each pump and may pop, with the money earned on the trial shown.

variants.name: BART-Y (Youth Version)
variants.note: A named children's instrument with points toward a prize, a simpler display and a progress meter; the pump-or-collect decision is unchanged.

variants.name: Variable Explosion Probability
variants.note: Balloon color signals which hidden pop schedule applies, so the participant learns within the session which colors are risky.

variants.name: Social Context BART
variants.note: The participant plays while observed, or sees how other people pumped, instead of playing alone.

variants.name: BART with Loss Domain
variants.note: Each balloon starts full of money and every pump removes some while raising the chance of a larger loss, so the same pump-or-stop structure is framed as accepting loss rather than chasing gain.

families.rationale: Sequential risk taking for reward

short_definition: Judgment of human action or identity from sparse point-light displays attached to major joints; indexes recognition of biological motion from kinematic cues alone.
description: Participants view point-light display stimuli, animations created by placing markers on the joints of a person performing actions and capturing only the light points. The resulting stimuli (12-15 dots representing joints) convey complex human actions (walking, running, dancing) from minimal motion cues. Participants may recognize actions, judge coherence (upright vs. inverted), or discriminate biological from scrambled motion. The task measures perception of complex human movement and activates the posterior superior temporal sulcus, a region specialized for biological motion processing.

procedure: Participants view point-light displays (dots at major joints) and identify actions, discriminate facing direction, or detect biological motion embedded in noise dots.
manipulations: Display type (intact, scrambled, inverted, reversed playback)
Comparison motion (mechanical vs. biological point-light motion)

short_definition: Learn target faces across viewpoints, then identify them among distractors under increasingly difficult conditions (novel viewpoints, visual noise); accuracy indexes face recognition ability and configural face processing.
description: The Cambridge Face Memory Test is the standard measure of face recognition ability for both clinical and individual-difference research. Participants study six target faces shown in three different viewpoints. Testing occurs in three phases of increasing difficulty: in Phase 1, targets are tested in studied viewpoints; in Phase 2, targets appear in novel viewpoints and lighting conditions; in Phase 3, Gaussian visual noise is added to the images. Each phase has 12 trials (one target face among five distractor faces), yielding a total score of 72. The CFMT specifically indexes holistic and configural face processing, is relatively culture-fair, and has become the benchmark for diagnosing prosopagnosia and studying "super-recognizers."

procedure: Participants learn a set of target faces during study, then identify them among distractor faces in increasingly difficult test phases (same image, novel viewpoint, plus noise).
manipulations: Test phase difficulty (same view, novel view, contrast-degraded)

material: Six target faces in three viewpoints, tested among distractor faces in the studied views, in novel views and lighting, and with added visual noise.

short_definition: Brief sample array followed after a blank delay by a probe array; participant reports whether any item changed. Yields visual working memory capacity (K).
description: The Change Detection Task, developed by Luck and Vogel (1997), is the standard paradigm for measuring visual working memory capacity. Participants briefly view a memory array of colored squares (typically 100-500 ms), followed by a blank retention interval (~900 ms), then a test array. On half the trials, one item changes color; participants report whether a change occurred. Performance is converted to a capacity estimate (K) using Cowan's formula: K = set size x (hit rate - false alarm rate). The task established that visual WM capacity is approximately 3-4 items in healthy adults and has been instrumental in research linking WM capacity to attention, intelligence, and neural oscillations.

procedure: A brief memory array of colored squares (or oriented bars) is followed by a retention interval and a test array.
Participants indicate whether a change occurred.
measurements: Accuracy converted to capacity estimate K (Cowan's K or Pashler's K)

material: Arrays of colored squares (or oriented bars) in which one item may change color between the memory array and the test array.

variants.name: Single-Probe Change Detection
variants.note: Only one square reappears at one of the original locations and the same/different judgment is about that item alone rather than the whole array.

variants.name: Change Detection with Filtering
variants.note: The array includes items the participant is told by a feature cue to ignore (remember the red bars, not the blue), so the study instruction selects a cued subset of the array.

variants.name: Continuous Report / Precision Task
variants.note: One location is probed and the participant reproduces the remembered feature on a continuous scale such as a color wheel, instead of judging whether it changed; the spread of the errors measures memory precision.

families.rationale: Sample array, delay, probe array

short_definition: Visual search in which some distractor configurations repeat across blocks; faster search on repeated configurations indexes implicit spatial context learning.
description: Participants perform visual search for a T-shaped target among L-shaped distractors. Critically, half the search displays repeat across blocks (with the target always in the same location within a given repeated display), while the other half are newly generated on each block. Search becomes faster for repeated displays over blocks, even though participants cannot consciously recognize which displays have been repeated. Chun and Jiang (1998) demonstrated that this contextual cueing effect reflects implicit learning and memory for spatial configurations that guide spatial attention to the likely target location. The paradigm has become a standard tool for studying the interface between attention, implicit learning, and long-term memory.

procedure: Visual search through letter arrays.
Some spatial configurations repeat across blocks while others are novel.
Participants find and respond to a target embedded in the display.
Optional: After the learning blocks a test phase alters the repeated displays to see whether the speed-up survives.
manipulations: Display type (real-world scenes vs. letter arrays)
measurements: RT advantage for repeated over novel configurations (contextual cueing effect)

material: A T-shaped target among L-shaped distractors, in spatial configurations that either repeat across blocks or are new.

variants.name: Configuration-Based vs. Association-Based CC
variants.note: Either the whole layout repeats or only the pairing of target position with a few distractor positions, to see which is learned.

variants.name: Semantic Contextual Cueing
variants.note: The displays are photographs of real scenes with a target object placed in each, and the scenes repeat across blocks.

variants.name: Cross-Modal Contextual Cueing
variants.note: A sound or touch pattern, rather than the visual layout, is paired with the target location and search speeds up when it plays; the learned sound works as a location cue whose validity is discovered rather than instructed.

variants.name: Dynamic Contextual Cueing
variants.note: The search items move and what repeats is the motion pattern and the target's final position rather than a static layout.

variants.name: Transfer of Contextual Cueing
variants.note: After the learning blocks a test phase alters the repeated displays (the distractor identities, their number, or the target position) to see whether the speed-up survives.

families.rationale: Visual search with repeated layouts; the learning could argue for conditioning and implicit learning

short_definition: Extended stream of stimuli in which a rare target requires a response; omission and commission errors index sustained attention and response control.
description: The Continuous Performance Task requires participants to continuously monitor a stream of stimuli and respond selectively to infrequent target stimuli while withholding responses to non-targets over an extended period (5-15 minutes). The standard version involves responding when the letter "X" appears; the AX Continuous Performance Task, a separate task, requires responding only when "A" is immediately followed by "X." Target frequency is typically 5-25% of trials. Performance measures include hit rate, false alarm rate, d' (sensitivity), and vigilance decrement over time. The task is widely used in ADHD research and clinical neuropsychology.

procedure: A rapid sequence of stimuli is presented.
Participants respond to infrequent target stimuli and withhold responses to non-targets over a prolonged session (10-20 min).

material: A stream of single letters (or digits or tones) in which one item, usually the letter X, is the rare target.

variants.name: Identical Pairs CPT (IP-CPT)
variants.note: The target is any item identical to the one just before it, so each item is compared with the previous one instead of with a fixed letter.

variants.name: Gradual-Onset CPT (gradCPT)
variants.note: Scenes fade into one another with no gaps; the participant classifies each as city or mountain, pressing for the frequent category and withholding for the rare one.

variants.name: Auditory CPT
variants.note: The same rare-target detection with spoken letters or tones through headphones instead of letters on a screen.

variants.name: Conners' CPT-3
variants.note: A commercial instrument that reverses the usual go rate (press for every letter except X, withhold for X) and varies the pace between blocks.

variants.name: TOVA (Test of Variables of Attention)
variants.note: A commercial instrument with a position-defined shape target and a rare-then-frequent target probability across halves; a named form.

variants.name: CPT with Emotional Distractors
variants.note: Emotional pictures or faces appear in the background or between items as distractors while the usual rare-target detection continues.

short_definition: Experimenter taps a sequence on spatially arranged blocks; participant reproduces the sequence forward or backward. Indexes visuospatial short-term and working memory span.
description: The Corsi Block-Tapping Task measures visuospatial short-term and working memory. Nine blocks are arranged irregularly on a board (or screen). The examiner taps a sequence of blocks, and the participant reproduces the sequence. Sequence length increases from 2 blocks upward until the participant fails two consecutive sequences at a given length. The maximum reliably reproduced length defines the Corsi span, typically around 5-6 for healthy adults. The backward version requires reproducing sequences in reverse order, adding executive demands. The task is the spatial counterpart of Digit Span and is critical for understanding the visuospatial sketchpad component of working memory.

procedure: The experimenter (or computer) taps a sequence of blocks on a board.
The participant reproduces the sequence in the same (or reverse) order.
Sequence length increases until recall fails.

material: Nine blocks arranged irregularly on a board or screen, tapped in sequences of increasing length.

variants.name: Computerized (eCorsi)
variants.note: Squares on a screen light up in sequence and are touched or clicked in order, with each touch timed.

variants.name: Supra-Span Corsi
variants.note: One sequence longer than span is presented repeatedly until it is reproduced correctly, and the number of attempts is the score.

variants.name: Walking Corsi (large-scale)
variants.note: The blocks become tiles on the floor of a room, the examiner walks a route over them and the participant walks the same route.

variants.name: Sequential vs. Simultaneous Presentation
variants.note: In the simultaneous condition all blocks of a set are highlighted at once with numbers or arrows giving the order, instead of being tapped one after another, and the participant still reproduces them in order.

short_definition: Repeated choices between smaller-sooner and larger-later rewards at varying delays; indifference points estimate a temporal discount function.
description: Participants make repeated choices between a smaller immediate reward and a larger delayed reward (e.g., "$10 now or $25 in 1 week"). The immediate amount or delay is systematically varied to estimate indifference points, yielding a discount rate reflecting how steeply the subjective value of rewards declines with delay. Steeper discounting reflects greater impulsivity. fMRI reveals differential activation of ventromedial PFC and nucleus accumbens (immediate preference) versus dorsolateral PFC and posterior parietal cortex (delayed preference), supporting dual-system valuation models.

procedure: Participants choose between a smaller immediate reward and a larger delayed reward across many trials with varying amounts and delays.
manipulations: Choice procedure (adjusting amount, adjusting delay, fixed list)
Delay type (experienced, waited out vs. described)

material: Pairs of money offers, a smaller amount now against a larger amount after a delay (such as $10 now or $25 in 1 week).

variants.note: A named one-minute instrument that bisects the delay range in five fixed choices.

variants.name: Fixed-Choice Discrete Trials
variants.note: A fixed list of now-versus-later questions (for example the 27-item Monetary Choice Questionnaire) with no adjustment based on earlier answers.

variants.name: Magnitude Manipulation
variants.note: The whole procedure is run in separate blocks for small, medium and large reward magnitudes.

variants.name: Experiential Discounting Task
variants.note: Delays are seconds to a minute and are actually waited out, with the reward delivered after each wait, so outcomes are experienced rather than only described.

variants.name: Gain vs. Loss Framing
variants.note: Choices between paying a smaller amount now or a larger amount later are added alongside the usual gain choices.

variants.name: Probabilistic Discounting
variants.note: The larger reward is uncertain rather than delayed, so the choice trades amount against probability instead of against delay.

variants.name: Cross-Commodity Discounting
variants.note: The rewards are something other than money, or the two options are in different commodities, described in words.

families.rationale: Smaller-sooner versus larger-later choices

short_definition: Sample stimulus followed by a delay and then a probe or choice array; response indicates whether the probe matches the sample. Indexes short-term memory maintenance.
description: The Delayed Match-to-Sample (DMTS) task consists of three phases: sample, delay, and choice. During the sample phase, a stimulus is presented. Following a delay period (0-30 seconds), the participant must identify which of several test stimuli matches the original sample. Memory demands are manipulated by varying delay duration or the number of choice alternatives. The task has been fundamental in primate neuroscience for identifying the neural substrates of working memory, particularly delay-period persistent activity in prefrontal cortex.

procedure: A sample stimulus is presented, followed by a retention interval (delay), then a test stimulus.
Participants indicate whether the test matches the sample.
manipulations: Test rule (choose the non-match vs. the match)

material: A sample stimulus followed after a delay by test stimuli, one of which matches it.

variants.name: DMTS with Distraction During Delay
variants.note: Other pictures, sounds, or a brief secondary task fill the retention interval to test how well the memory withstands interference.

variants.name: Spatial DMTS
variants.note: The sample's location rather than its identity is remembered, and after the delay the participant indicates where it was or chooses between locations.

variants.name: DMTS with Object Complexity Manipulation
variants.note: Samples range from simple colored shapes to detailed hard-to-name patterns and accuracy is compared across complexity levels.

families.rationale: Sample, delay, match judgment

short_definition: One-shot allocation task in which a proposer unilaterally divides an endowment between self and a passive receiver; indexes altruism and social preferences.
description: One player (dictator) unilaterally decides how much of an endowment to give to an anonymous recipient, who has no power to reject. Despite having complete power, many dictators give 20-30% of their endowment, reflecting intrinsic fairness concerns. fMRI shows generous allocations activate reward regions (ventral striatum, OFC) and empathy regions (anterior insula, ACC), suggesting altruistic choices engage similar neural systems as personal reward.

procedure: Participants in the dictator role are endowed with a sum and decide how much (if any) to give to an anonymous recipient.
The recipient has no choice but to accept.
manipulations: Role structure (both players give and receive vs. one giver)
Exit option (opt out for a fixed payoff vs. none)

material: An endowment of money, of which the participant gives any share to an anonymous recipient.

variants.name: Double Dictator
variants.note: Both players are endowed and each decides at the same time how much to give the other, so every participant is both giver and recipient.

variants.name: Earned vs. Windfall Endowment
variants.note: The participant either earns the endowment in a prior task or is simply handed it before making the same allocation.

variants.name: Audience/Observation Effects
variants.note: The allocation is made where the experimenter or another person can see or will learn of it instead of under full anonymity.

variants.name: N-Person Dictator
variants.note: The money is divided among several recipients rather than one, possibly in different amounts.

variants.name: Charitable Giving Dictator
variants.note: The recipient is a named charity rather than an anonymous person, so the other party is an organization.

variants.name: Exit Option
variants.note: Before allocating, the participant may decline to play and keep a slightly smaller sum, and the recipient never learns that a game existed.

families.rationale: Unilateral allocation to a passive receiver

short_definition: Auditory or visual digit sequences reproduced in forward or backward order; longest correctly reproduced length indexes verbal short-term and working memory span.
description: The Digit Span task measures verbal short-term and working memory capacity. In the Forward condition, participants listen to sequences of digits presented at a rate of one per second and immediately repeat them in the same order; sequence length increases until recall fails. In the Backward condition, participants repeat digits in reverse order, adding a manipulation component. The Sequencing condition (from WAIS-IV) requires reordering digits numerically. Digit Span is one of the oldest and most widely administered neuropsychological measures, embedded in the Wechsler intelligence and memory scales. Forward span primarily indexes the phonological loop, while backward span engages central executive processes.

procedure: Sequences of digits are presented at a rate of one per second.
Participants reproduce the sequence in forward, backward, or sequencing order.
Length increases until two consecutive failures.
manipulations: Task instruction (keep only the most recent items vs. report all)
List presentation (grouped by pauses vs. even pace)
Stimulus type (spatial grid sequence vs. digits)
measurements: Forward-backward difference as index of executive load

material: Spoken sequences of digits, one per second, growing longer until recall fails.

variants.name: Letter-Number Sequencing
variants.note: The list mixes letters and digits and the participant reports the digits in ascending order then the letters in alphabetical order, the sequencing direction applied twice to one list.

variants.name: Auditory vs. Visual Presentation
variants.note: The digits are shown one at a time on a screen instead of being spoken, and are said or typed back.

variants.name: Adaptive Staircase Versions
variants.note: A computer sets each list length from recent accuracy instead of running the fixed ascending series, and span is read from where performance settles.

variants.name: Spatial Digit Span
variants.note: Each digit appears at a different screen position and the participant reproduces the digits in order, sometimes also reporting where each one appeared, which binds a location to each item.

variants.name: Running Digit Span
variants.note: Lists stop at an unpredictable point and only the last few digits are reported, so the participant keeps only the most recent items and drops older ones as new ones arrive.

variants.name: Matrix Span
variants.note: A sequence of cells lights up in a grid and the participant indicates the cells in the order shown, a spatial counterpart of digit span.

variants.name: Supra-Span Lists
variants.note: One list longer than span is repeated until recalled perfectly, so the study-test cycle repeats to a criterion and the number of repetitions is the score.

families.rationale: Reproduce a digit sequence

short_definition: Timed paper-and-pencil or computerized task: substitute digits for symbols (or vice versa) using a visible key; items completed in a fixed interval index processing speed.
description: The Digit Symbol Substitution Test (also known as Symbol Digit Modalities Test, SDMT, in its symbol-to-digit variant) is one of the most sensitive neuropsychological measures of processing speed and cognitive efficiency. Participants view a key pairing digits 1-9 with unique abstract symbols. They then fill in the corresponding symbol for each digit in a series (DSST) or write the digit for each symbol (SDMT), working as quickly and accurately as possible for 90-120 seconds. The number of correct substitutions is the primary score. The DSST/SDMT is included in the WAIS and is among the most sensitive tests for detecting cognitive impairment from neurological conditions, medication side effects, and normal aging.

procedure: A key pairs digits 1-9 with unique symbols.
Participants fill in the correct symbol below each digit in a long sequence, working as quickly as possible for 90-120 seconds.
measurements: Number of correct substitutions in the time limit

material: A key pairing the digits 1-9 with abstract symbols, and a long series of digits (or symbols) to fill in.

variants.name: SDMT (Symbol-to-Digit; Smith)
variants.note: A named instrument that reverses the lookup direction, so the rows show symbols and the participant writes the paired digit.

variants.name: Oral SDMT
variants.note: The participant says each digit aloud and the examiner writes it down.

variants.name: Computerized DSST/SDMT
variants.note: Items appear one at a time on a screen and each key press or tap brings the next, so the continuous page becomes a series of self-paced discrete trials timed individually.

variants.name: Paired-Associate Variant
variants.note: After the timed substitution the key is removed and the participant is asked without warning which symbol went with each digit, adding a surprise cued-recall test of the pairs.

families.rationale: Speeded symbol coding; processing speed rather than motor control is the usual reading

short_definition: Study-phase cues instruct participants to remember or forget specific items or lists; later memory tests index intentional forgetting.
description: Participants study items (typically words) under instructions that each item should either be remembered or forgotten. In the item method, a remember or forget cue follows each individual item. In the list method, a single cue midway through the study phase instructs participants to forget everything studied so far. On a subsequent memory test, recall and recognition of forget-cued items is impaired relative to remember-cued items. The paradigm provides the primary laboratory tool for studying intentional forgetting and memory control, with theoretical implications for understanding inhibitory control over memory, context change, and selective rehearsal.

procedure: Items are presented one at a time or in lists.
After each item (item method) or after a full list (list method), a cue instructs the participant to remember or forget it.
A final test probes all items.
Optional: The final test is old/new recognition among new words rather than free recall.
Optional: At test the participant also says which cue each recognized word received or which list it came from.
manipulations: Study task (performing the action vs. reading the phrase)
measurements: Recall/recognition accuracy for remember-cued vs. forget-cued items

material: Lists of words, each word (or the list) followed by a cue to remember or to forget it.

variants.name: List-Method Directed Forgetting
variants.note: The cue comes once after a whole first list instead of after each item, a second list is studied, and the final test covers both lists.

variants.name: Recognition vs. Recall Test
variants.note: The final test is old/new recognition among new words rather than free recall.

variants.name: Directed Forgetting with Source Memory
variants.note: At test the participant also says which cue each recognized word received or which list it came from, so the test is a source judgment rather than plain recall.

variants.name: Emotional Directed Forgetting
variants.note: Emotional words or pictures are studied alongside neutral ones and the forgetting effect is compared across valence.

variants.name: Directed Forgetting of Actions (SPT)
variants.note: The items are action phrases that the participant performs with real objects at study, before each is cued to be remembered or forgotten, instead of only reading them.

variants.name: Cumulative Directed Forgetting
variants.note: Several lists are studied in a row, each followed by its own remember or forget cue, before one final test.

families.rationale: Remember or forget cues at study

short_definition: A pair of cues (often threat/neutral) is followed by a probe at one cue location; RT difference by cue type indexes attentional bias.
description: The Dot-Probe Task measures attentional bias toward or away from emotionally salient stimuli. On each trial, a pair of stimuli (e.g., one threatening face and one neutral face) appears briefly (typically 500 ms), followed by a probe (dot or arrow) at the location of one stimulus. Participants respond to the probe (detect or classify it). Attentional bias is inferred from faster responses to probes replacing the emotional stimulus (vigilance toward threat) versus slower responses (avoidance). The task is a cornerstone of research on anxiety-related attentional biases and has been central to Attentional Bias Modification (ABM) treatments.

procedure: Two stimuli (e.g., a threatening face and a neutral face) appear briefly on screen.
One is replaced by a probe (dot or letter) that participants locate or classify.
manipulations: Probe location (congruent with threat vs. incongruent)
Stimulus type (faces, words, scenes or objects)
measurements: RT difference between congruent and incongruent probe trials (attentional bias score)

material: Pairs of stimuli, typically a threatening and a neutral face (threat, positive or neutral), followed by a dot or arrow probe at the location of one of them.

combined_with.note: Gaze is held on the fixation target while the main game is played.

variants.name: Word Dot-Probe
variants.note: A threat word and a neutral word form the pair instead of faces.

variants.name: Pictorial Dot-Probe
variants.note: Emotional and neutral photographs of scenes or objects form the pair instead of faces or words.

variants.name: Detection vs. Classification Probe
variants.note: The probe job is either a single press when the probe appears (detect) or a report of which of two probe forms appeared (classify), replacing the standard localization.

families.rationale: Probe appears at one of two cue locations

short_definition: View affective images under instructions to reappraise or passively view; self-reported affect, physiological responses, and neural activity index emotion regulation ability.
description: Participants view emotionally evocative stimuli (typically IAPS images) and are instructed to either passively view them ("look" condition) or regulate their emotional response using cognitive reappraisal (e.g., reinterpreting a car accident as a movie scene). After each trial, participants rate their emotional experience. Reappraisal successfully reduces subjective negative affect and modulates neural activity: it increases dorsolateral and ventrolateral PFC activation while decreasing amygdala activation, demonstrating top-down prefrontal regulation of emotion generation systems.

procedure: Participants view emotionally evocative images and are instructed to regulate their emotional response using a specified strategy (e.g., cognitive reappraisal, suppression, or distraction) or to simply attend.
manipulations: Regulation strategy (reappraise, distance, suppress, distract, accept, attend)
Exposure control (choice or early termination vs. assigned exposure)

material: Emotionally evocative photographs, typically from the IAPS, of negative or positive valence.

variants.name: Distraction/Attentional Deployment
variants.note: A second task (mental arithmetic or letter memory) runs while the picture is on screen, so regulation works through the competing task rather than an instruction about the picture.

combined_with.note: An arithmetic or letter task is done during viewing.

variants.name: Expressive Suppression
variants.note: The instruction is to keep face and body still while viewing a picture or film clip.

variants.name: Situation Selection/Modification
variants.note: The participant chooses which picture or clip to be exposed to or ends a clip early, so regulation happens through choice over exposure rather than through a stance toward a stimulus already present.

variants.name: Up-Regulation
variants.note: The participant is told to make the feeling stronger rather than weaker.

variants.name: Implicit Emotion Regulation
variants.note: No regulation instruction is given; regulation is inferred from responses after a self-control prime or from spontaneous recovery.

families.rationale: Reappraise or passively view affective images

short_definition: Color-naming of emotionally valenced words; RT slowing on threat-related words indexes attentional bias to affective content.
description: A variant of the classic Stroop in which participants name the ink color of words that vary in emotional valence (threat-related, positive, neutral). Emotional interference is measured as the slowing of color naming for emotional relative to neutral words, indexing the degree to which emotional content captures attentional resources. The task is widely used in anxiety and PTSD research, where threat-related words produce disproportionate interference. The emotional interference effect reflects automatic processing of affectively significant information.

procedure: Color words are replaced by emotionally valenced or threat-related words.
Participants name the ink color while ignoring word meaning.
manipulations: Word valence/threat relevance (disorder-specific, general threat, positive, neutral)
Awareness of the emotional word (subliminal masked prime vs. visible)
measurements: RT slowing for threat/emotional words relative to neutral (emotional Stroop interference)

material: Emotionally valenced or threat-related words (disorder-specific, general threat or neutral) printed in colored ink.

variants.name: Disorder-Specific Variants
variants.note: The emotional word set is matched to the clinical concern of a patient group; the color-naming procedure is unchanged.

variants.name: Pictorial Emotional Stroop
variants.note: Emotional and neutral pictures carry a colored border or tint and the participant names that color while ignoring the picture.

variants.name: Subliminal Emotional Stroop
variants.note: The word is flashed below awareness and then covered by a colored mask whose color is named, so the emotional word acts as a masked prime before the judged item rather than as part of it.

variants.name: Face-Word Emotional Stroop
variants.note: An emotion word is written across an expressive face and the participant names the expression while ignoring the word (or the reverse), so the competitor is now response-mapped as in the color-word Stroop.

families.rationale: Stroop procedure with emotional words

short_definition: A central target flanked by congruent or incongruent distractors; RT and error differences index selective attention and conflict resolution.
description: The Eriksen Flanker Task measures selective attention and the ability to inhibit responses to irrelevant flanking stimuli. Participants view a brief display of five items arranged horizontally, with a central target flanked by two non-target items on each side. The central target requires a specific response, while flanking items may be congruent (same response), incongruent (opposite response), or neutral. Participants respond via speeded button press while ignoring flankers. The flanker compatibility effect (slowed RT and increased errors on incongruent trials) indexes the degree of response competition and the efficiency of attentional filtering.

procedure: Participants identify a central target (arrow or letter) flanked by congruent, incongruent, or neutral distractors.
manipulations: Stimulus type (arrows, letters, color patches, digits, emotional faces or pictures)
Added no-go signal on a minority of trials

material: A row of five items, a central arrow or letter between flankers that call for the same response, the opposite response or neither.

variants.name: Letter Flanker
variants.note: Letters replace arrows with an arbitrary letter-to-key mapping; the original 1974 form.

variants.name: Color Flanker
variants.note: The response is to the color of a central patch while flanking patches share the color or carry the other response's color.

variants.name: Emotional Flanker
variants.note: The central item and flankers are expressive faces or pictures and the participant classifies the central emotion.

variants.name: Numerical Flanker
variants.note: Digits replace arrows and the participant classifies the central digit against a boundary (larger or smaller than 5) while flanking digits fall on the same or the other side.

variants.name: Combined Flanker + Go/No-Go
variants.note: On a minority of trials a display feature signals that no response should be made, so responding is withheld under flanker conflict.

families.rationale: Target with congruent or incongruent flankers

short_definition: Blocked or event-related presentation of faces vs. objects (or scrambled faces) to localize face-selective cortical regions (FFA, OFA, pSTS).
description: The FFA Localizer presents alternating blocks of faces and non-face objects (houses, cars, scrambled images) while participants perform passive viewing or a simple task (one-back matching, gender judgment). The contrast of faces > objects identifies face-selective regions, particularly the fusiform face area (FFA) in ventral temporal cortex. The task provides an individually-defined localizer for face-selective cortex and has been fundamental to understanding the neural basis of face perception and the question of domain-specific processing modules.

procedure: Blocks of faces alternate with blocks of non-face objects (houses, scrambled images) while participants perform a simple repetition-detection task.
The contrast localizes face-selective cortex.
manipulations: Stimulus category (faces, objects, scrambled, scenes, inverted faces, face parts)
Stimulus format (dynamic video vs. still photograph)
Face familiarity (known or famous vs. unknown)
measurements: fMRI contrast (faces > objects) identifying FFA, OFA, STS
Extent and magnitude of face-selective activation

material: Blocks of face photographs alternating with blocks of non-face objects such as houses, cars or scrambled images.

variants.name: Dynamic Face Localizer
variants.note: Short video clips of moving faces and moving objects replace still photographs.

variants.name: Identity Adaptation
variants.note: Faces are shown in pairs or short runs in which identity repeats or changes trial by trial, and the response reduction to a repeat is the measure instead of a block contrast.

variants.name: Familiar vs. Unfamiliar Faces
variants.note: Some faces belong to people the participant knows or to famous people, and responses to known and unknown faces are compared.

families.rationale: Passive presentation of faces versus objects to isolate a perceptual response

short_definition: Identification of an emotion category from a face image; accuracy and RT per emotion index emotion decoding ability.
description: Participants view photographs of facial expressions (typically from the Ekman and Friesen Pictures of Facial Affect or similar validated sets) and identify the emotion portrayed. The standard set includes six basic emotions (anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise) plus neutral. Accuracy and RT are measured across emotion categories. The task engages a network including the amygdala (particularly for fear), fusiform face area, superior temporal sulcus, and prefrontal cortex. It is widely used in clinical research on schizophrenia, autism, and mood disorders.

procedure: Participants view face photographs displaying basic emotions and identify the expressed emotion from a fixed set (happy, sad, angry, fearful, disgusted, surprised, neutral).
manipulations: Stimulus format (dynamic video vs. still photograph)
Context cue (congruent or conflicting body posture or scene)

material: Photographs of faces of varying race and gender showing one of six basic emotions or a neutral expression, from validated sets such as Ekman and Friesen's.

variants.name: Dynamic Expressions
variants.note: The face is a short video unfolding from neutral to full expression instead of a still photograph.

variants.name: Emotion-in-Context
variants.note: A body posture or scene that agrees or conflicts with the expression accompanies the face, so there is now a neighbouring item to disregard while labelling the face.

variants.name: Expression Matching
variants.note: The participant decides whether two faces show the same expression, or picks the match to a target face, instead of naming a category.

variants.name: Dimensional Ratings
variants.note: The participant places each face on continuous scales (pleasantness, arousal) instead of choosing an emotion category.

short_definition: Wimmer & Perner-style narrative in which a protagonist holds a belief the participant knows to be false; correct prediction of the protagonist's action indexes mentalizing.
description: The False Belief Task assesses the ability to attribute mental states to others that differ from reality. In the classic Sally-Anne version, Sally places an object in location A and leaves; Anne moves the object to location B. Participants are asked where Sally will look for the object. Correct performance (location A) requires representing Sally's false belief rather than the true state of the world. Adult neuroimaging versions use animated vignettes requiring belief reasoning. fMRI consistently activates medial prefrontal cortex, precuneus, and right temporoparietal junction.

procedure: Participants hear or read vignettes in which a character holds a belief that conflicts with reality (e.g., Sally-Anne scenario), then predict the character's behavior.
manipulations: True belief vs. false belief conditions
Story type (unexpected contents vs. moved object)
Belief structure (two differing beliefs, neither false)
Task type (animated shapes described vs. false belief question)
Story format (text, speech or cartoon vs. acted with props)
Competition (planting a false belief against an opponent)
measurements: Accuracy on false-belief vs. true-belief questions

material: Short stories, told, read or acted out with pictures or objects, in which a character believes an object is where it no longer is (the Sally-Anne scenario).

variants.name: Implicit False Belief (Looking Time)
variants.note: Infants watch an actor search where the actor should believe the object is or where it really is, and looking time is recorded; no question is asked.

variants.name: Anticipatory Looking
variants.note: The answer is where the participant looks just before the character acts, recorded by an eye tracker, instead of a spoken answer.

variants.name: Animated Triangles (Heider-Simmel)
variants.note: The participant watches shapes move as if with intentions and describes what happened, scored for mental-state language; there is no false belief and no correct answer.

variants.name: Cartoon/Story Vignette Tasks
variants.note: The false-belief story is given as text, speech or a cartoon strip rather than acted with props.

variants.name: Adult False Belief with Reaction Time
variants.note: Adults answer many short scenarios by speeded key press, so the answer is a choice among keys and response time is the measure.

variants.name: Competitive False Belief (Deception)
variants.note: The participant plays against a real opponent and wins by planting a false belief, for example by pointing to the wrong hiding place, so the answer becomes a move in a game rather than a report.

combined_with.note: The belief worked out decides the move against an opponent.

families.rationale: Predict behavior from a protagonist's false belief

short_definition: Repetitive single-finger or sequence tapping at fastest or paced rates; taps-per-interval and tap-timing variability index motor speed and rhythm control.
description: Participants tap their fingers (typically index finger) in a repetitive manner at a self-paced or externally paced rate. Self-paced tapping is typically at 2-3 Hz; externally paced versions use an auditory or visual metronome. The task consists of tapping blocks (20-40 seconds) alternating with rest periods. Performance metrics include tapping frequency, inter-tap interval variability, and accuracy. It is the most commonly used simple motor paradigm for motor cortex mapping, clinical motor assessment, and studying motor control. Contralateral primary motor cortex and supplementary motor area are consistently activated.

procedure: Participants tap a key or button with a single finger as rapidly as possible (maximum rate) or in synchrony with a metronome (paced tapping).
manipulations: Tapping pattern (unequal rhythm vs. even beat)
measurements: Synchronization error and drift in paced conditions

material: A metronome beat (a tone or a light) to tap in time with, in the paced form; the self-paced form presents nothing.

variants.name: Auditorily-Paced Tapping
variants.note: The participant taps in time with a metronome click, so pacing is external.

variants.name: Visually-Paced Tapping
variants.note: The pacing signal is a flashing shape on a screen instead of a sound.

variants.name: Unimanual vs. Bimanual
variants.note: Both hands tap at once, in unison or alternating, instead of one hand.

variants.name: Sequential Multi-Finger
variants.note: A fixed order of fingers is tapped over and over instead of one finger repeating.

variants.name: Complex Rhythmic Patterns
variants.note: One finger reproduces a rhythm with unequal intervals (long-short-short) rather than tapping an even beat.

variants.name: Continuation Paradigm
variants.note: The participant taps along with a metronome, then keeps the same rate unaided after it stops.

families.rationale: Tapping rate and timing

short_definition: Study of a list of items followed by unaided recall in any order; serial-position curves dissociate primacy and recency.
description: Participants study a list of items (typically words) presented sequentially, then attempt to recall all items in any order during an extended recall period. Performance is analyzed via serial position curves showing primacy effects (enhanced recall of early items, attributed to long-term memory consolidation) and recency effects (enhanced recall of recent items, attributed to short-term memory). Clustering analyses examine whether semantically or contextually related items are recalled together, revealing the organization of memory search. The task engages prefrontal, parietal, and temporal memory networks.

procedure: Participants study a list of items (words, pictures) presented one at a time, then recall as many as possible in any order after the last item.
Optional: After many lists have each been studied and recalled, the participant is asked without warning to recall every word from every list.
Optional: The same list is recalled several times in succession without being studied again.
manipulations: Distractor interval (after every study item vs. before recall only)

material: A list of words (or pictures) presented one at a time, its semantic organization varied.

variants.name: Delayed Free Recall (DFR)
variants.note: A filled delay of 15 to 30 seconds of mental arithmetic is inserted between the end of the list and recall.

variants.name: Final Free Recall
variants.note: After many lists have each been studied and recalled, the participant is unexpectedly asked to recall every word from every list.

variants.name: Externalized Free Recall
variants.note: The participant says every word that comes to mind, including ones they believe are wrong, and flags each one they reject.

families.rationale: Study a list, recall in any order

short_definition: Responses required to frequent "go" stimuli must be withheld on rare "no-go" stimuli; commission errors and N2/P3 ERPs index response inhibition.
description: The Go/No-Go Task measures response inhibition by requiring participants to respond quickly to frequent "go" stimuli while withholding responses to infrequent "no-go" stimuli. The typical ratio is 70-80% go and 20-30% no-go trials, creating a strong prepotent tendency to respond. Performance is measured by go-trial RT (engagement), go-trial accuracy (compliance), and no-go accuracy / false alarm rate (inhibitory control). The task is simpler than the Stop-Signal task as it measures the ability to withhold (rather than cancel) a response.

procedure: Stimuli appear one at a time.
Participants respond (Go) to frequent targets and withhold (No-Go) responses to infrequent non-targets.
manipulations: Incentive cue and outcome (win vs. avoid loss, by action)
Cue before each stimulus (predicting go or no-go)
Flankers around the go or no-go item
Reversal of go and no-go roles (signaled vs. unsignaled)
Number of go and no-go stimuli (mapping size)
measurements: No-Go N2 and P3 ERP components

material: A series of single stimuli, typically letters, of which 70-80% are go items and the rest no-go items.

variants.name: Emotional Go/No-Go
variants.note: Go and no-go are defined by facial expression or emotional word, with the assignment reversed in other blocks; the structure is unchanged.

variants.name: Reward/Punishment Go/No-Go
variants.note: Each stimulus signals which of four action-by-outcome cells applies (go or no-go, to win or to avoid loss), so the stimulus carries an incentive cue and outcomes are paid per trial.

variants.name: Probabilistic Go/No-Go
variants.note: The go proportion is set per block from 50 to 90 percent; this is the ratio manipulation run in blocks.

variants.name: Cued Go/No-Go
variants.note: A cue before each stimulus says whether a go or a no-go stimulus is likely.

variants.name: Flanked Go/No-Go
variants.note: The go or no-go item is surrounded by congruent or incongruent flankers, adding neighbouring items as a competitor.

variants.name: Reversal Go/No-Go
variants.note: Partway through, go and no-go stimuli swap roles, with or without warning; coded as an unsignalled shift, but switches_on_cue applies when the swap is announced.

variants.name: Saccadic Go/No-Go
variants.note: The go response is an eye movement to the target and no-go means holding fixation; only the effector and recording device change.

families.rationale: Withhold on rare no-go stimuli

short_definition: Speeded categorization of stimuli belonging to two target concepts and two evaluative attributes using shared response keys; congruence-condition RT difference indexes implicit association.
description: Participants rapidly classify stimuli from four categories using two response keys. Two categories are target concepts (e.g., "flowers" vs. "insects") and two are evaluative attributes (e.g., "pleasant" vs. "unpleasant"). In the critical comparison, one block pairs congruent categories on the same key (flowers + pleasant) and another pairs incongruent categories (flowers + unpleasant). The IAT effect - faster responding in the congruent block - is interpreted as reflecting the strength of automatic associations between the concepts and attributes. Greenwald et al. (1998) introduced the IAT as a measure of implicit attitudes, and it has become one of the most widely administered psychological tests, with applications spanning racial bias, self-esteem, clinical anxiety, consumer preferences, and political attitudes.

procedure: Participants sort stimuli from two target categories (e.g., Black/White faces) and two attribute categories (e.g., pleasant/unpleasant words) using two response keys.
Critical comparison is between compatible and incompatible pairings.
manipulations: Number of practice and test trials
Number of target categories (single-category vs. two-category)
Response mapping (four keys, cued per trial vs. fixed per block)
measurements: IAT D-score (standardized RT difference between incompatible and compatible blocks)

material: Exemplars of two target categories (such as flowers and insects, or Black and White faces) and two attribute categories (pleasant and unpleasant words).

variants.name: Gender-Science IAT
variants.note: Male and female names or faces are paired with science and liberal-arts words, so the contrast measures a gender-field stereotype rather than valence.

variants.name: Self-Esteem IAT
variants.note: Self and other pronouns replace the social target categories, paired with pleasant and unpleasant words.

variants.name: Brief IAT (BIAT)
variants.note: A named shorter instrument in which each block has two focal categories on one key and everything else on the other.

variants.name: Go/No-Go Association Task (GNAT)
variants.note: The participant presses one key for items in the target pairing and withholds for everything else, so detection sensitivity replaces the two-key sort.

variants.name: Recoding-Free IAT (IAT-RF)
variants.note: Four keys, one per category, and a per-trial instruction says which keys are relevant, so the mapping is cued trial by trial instead of fixed for a block.

variants.name: Developmental / Child IAT
variants.note: All categories are pictures, instructions are spoken, there are fewer trials, and children sort on large buttons or a touch screen.

families.rationale: Response-key compatibility effect between paired categories

short_definition: Actions are reinforced by contingent outcomes under defined schedules; response rate and choice probability across schedules index instrumental learning. Specific human instantiations include lever/button-press reward paradigms and free-operant tasks.
description: In instrumental conditioning, voluntary actions are associated with rewarding or punishing consequences through repeated experience. Laboratory implementations present discrete choice options where specific responses are followed by desirable outcomes (food, money, points) or undesirable outcomes (loss, punishment). Common schedules include fixed-ratio, variable-ratio, fixed-interval, and variable-interval. Performance measures include response rates, choice patterns, and reaction times. The ventral striatum, dopamine system, and orbitofrontal cortex are critical for representing value predictions and learning from outcomes.

procedure: Participants perform actions (button presses, lever responses) that produce contingent outcomes (rewards or punishments) according to defined reinforcement schedules.
Optional: After training, the earned outcome is made less desirable and responding is tested without reward.
manipulations: Reinforcement schedule (fixed ratio, variable ratio, fixed interval, variable interval, progressive ratio)
measurements: Sensitivity to contingency and outcome devaluation
Transfer effects between Pavlovian cues and instrumental actions

material: Choice options whose responses are followed, on a reinforcement schedule, by rewards (food, money, points) or losses.

variants.name: Progressive Ratio
variants.note: The response requirement rises after each reward and the participant may quit at any time, so the schedule becomes a single escalating option with a stop decision; progressive ratio is not among the listed schedule levels.

variants.name: Concurrent Choice
variants.note: Two or more response options are available at once, each on its own schedule, so the participant allocates responses among options with hidden payoff rates.

variants.name: Devaluation Paradigm
variants.note: After training, the earned outcome is made less desirable and responding is tested without reward.

variants.name: Contingency Degradation
variants.note: After training, the reward is delivered whether or not the participant responds.

variants.name: Outcome-Specific Pavlovian-Instrumental Transfer (PIT)
variants.note: A separate Pavlovian phase of cue-outcome pairings is added, and a final transfer test presents the cues during free responding.

variants.name: Avoidance Learning
variants.note: The response prevents an unpleasant outcome (shock, noise, loss of money) instead of earning a reward.

families.rationale: Actions reinforced under a schedule

short_definition: Repeated choices among four decks with hidden reward and loss distributions; preference shift toward advantageous decks indexes affective decision making.
description: Participants choose cards from four decks to maximize winnings. Two decks (A, B) have high wins but higher losses (net loss); two decks (C, D) have smaller wins but minimal losses (net gain). Over 100 trials, healthy participants gradually learn to prefer advantageous decks. The IGT is particularly sensitive to ventromedial prefrontal cortex damage; vmPFC patients fail to develop a preference for advantageous decks despite normal intellectual functioning. The task operationalizes the Somatic Marker Hypothesis.

procedure: Four decks of cards are presented.
Participants draw one card at a time from any deck.
Each draw yields a reward and sometimes a penalty.
Two decks are advantageous (smaller rewards, smaller penalties, net positive) and two are disadvantageous (larger rewards, larger penalties, net negative).
manipulations: Outcome information (stated probabilities vs. discovered by experience)

material: Four decks of cards, each draw showing a money win and sometimes a loss, two decks with large wins and larger losses and two with small wins and small losses.

variants.note: Named children's instruments (Hungry Donkey, Children's Gambling Task) with a cartoon character, fewer trials and simpler feedback on the same payoff structure.

variants.name: IGT with Explicit Probabilities
variants.note: The win and loss amounts and probabilities of each deck are stated before play, so the options are described rather than discovered.

short_definition: Speeded word/nonword judgment; RT and accuracy index lexical access and are sensitive to frequency, priming, and context.
description: Participants view letter strings and must rapidly determine whether each string is a valid word or a nonword by pressing designated response buttons. Stimuli include high- and low-frequency words and pronounceable nonwords. RT and accuracy to words versus nonwords indexes lexical access efficiency. The task is often combined with priming manipulations to examine semantic, phonological, or morphological processing. It is one of the most fundamental paradigms in psycholinguistics.

procedure: Letter strings are presented one at a time.
Participants classify each as a real word or a nonword as quickly and accurately as possible.
manipulations: Language mix (words from two languages in one list)

material: Letter strings that are real words, varying in frequency, length and orthographic neighborhood, or nonwords that are pronounceable or random.

variants.name: Auditory LDT
variants.note: The items are spoken through headphones instead of printed; the word/nonword decision is unchanged.

variants.name: Masked Priming LDT
variants.note: A prime word is flashed for about 50 ms between masks before each target, adding a preceding prime whose relatedness to the target is varied.

variants.name: Cross-Modal LDT
variants.note: A spoken prime (word or sentence) is played before or during a printed target, or the reverse, adding a prime in a second modality.

variants.name: LDT with Different Nonword Types
variants.note: The nonwords are made more or less word-like (pseudohomophones, transposed-letter strings, consonant strings); the decision is unchanged and nonword type is the difficulty factor.

variants.name: Bilingual LDT
variants.note: Words from two of the participant's languages are mixed in one list and the decision is "a word in either language" or "a word in the named language"; the classification structure is unchanged.

variants.name: Go/No-Go LDT
variants.note: The participant presses for one class (words) and withholds for the other, instead of having a key for each.

families.rationale: Word versus nonword judgment

short_definition: Judgment of whether two rotated objects are identical or mirror images; RT scales linearly with angular disparity, indexing mental rotation.
description: Participants view pairs of 3D objects (block figures, letters, or geometric forms) and determine whether they are identical (one is a rotated version of the other) or mirror images. Objects are rotated at angles ranging from 0 to 180 degrees relative to each other. The well-established finding is that RT increases linearly with angular disparity, suggesting an analog mental rotation process. The task measures spatial visualization ability, mental imagery, and visuospatial working memory. Sex differences in mental rotation are among the most reliable cognitive sex differences.

procedure: Two figures (3-D block shapes, letters, or hands) are presented at different orientations.
Participants judge whether they are the same or mirror-reversed.
manipulations: Angular disparity between the two figures (0-180 degrees)
Task rule (hand laterality judgment vs. same-or-mirror comparison)
Concurrent movement (hand rotation congruent or incongruent with the imagined rotation)
measurements: RT as a function of angular disparity (linear slope = rotation rate)

material: Pairs of 2D or 3D figures (block figures, letters or hands) rotated relative to each other, identical or mirror-reversed.

variants.name: 2D Shape Rotation
variants.note: Flat letters, digits or polygons are rotated in the picture plane and a single rotated item is judged normal or mirror-reversed against its remembered canonical form, instead of being compared with a partner on screen.

variants.name: Body Part Rotation (Hand Laterality)
variants.note: A single picture of a hand in some orientation is classified as left or right, instead of two pictures being compared as same or mirrored.

variants.name: Mirror vs. Identical Discrimination
variants.note: One rotated figure is shown per trial and judged as the standard or its mirror image, so the comparison is against a figure held in memory.

variants.name: Embodied/Motor-Assisted Rotation
variants.note: While judging, the participant turns a handle or rotates the hand in the same or the opposite direction as the imagined rotation; whether the two directions agree is the factor of interest.

combined_with.note: A hand movement is made while the rotation judgment is formed.

variants.name: Virtual Reality Mental Rotation
variants.note: The objects are rendered in stereoscopic 3D through a head-mounted display and may be walked around or handled; the same-or-mirror judgment is unchanged.

variants.name: Egocentric vs. Allocentric Rotation
variants.note: In one condition the participant imagines turning themselves to a new viewpoint and reports what they would see; in the other they imagine the object turning while staying still.

families.rationale: Rotate objects mentally; could be filed under perceptual judgment

short_definition: Tracing of a figure viewed only in a mirror; error and completion time across trials index visuomotor adaptation and procedural learning.
description: The Mirror Tracing Task measures procedural motor learning and sensorimotor adaptation. Participants trace a shape (typically a star outline) while viewing their hand only through a mirror, which reverses the visual feedback left-right. This creates a conflict between visual and proprioceptive information that must be resolved through practice. Performance improves across trials as participants learn to adapt their motor commands to the reversed visual input. Measures include tracing time, number of errors (deviations from the path), and the rate of improvement across trials. The task is a classic demonstration that procedural/implicit memory is preserved in amnesia (H.M. could learn this task despite profound declarative memory loss).

procedure: Participants trace a path (star, maze) while viewing their hand only through a mirror, which reverses visual-motor mapping.
They must stay within path boundaries.
Optional: Tracing is practiced in one session and retested hours or days later with no practice between.
manipulations: Visuomotor mapping (left-right mirror, up-down or two-axis mirror, rotation)
Visual field shift (prism goggles; reach to targets)

material: A path to trace, such as a star outline or a maze, with the hand seen only in a mirror.

variants.name: Computerized Mirror Tracing
variants.note: The reversal is done in software with a mouse or stylus, with no physical mirror and no felt contact with the track edge.

variants.name: Rotation (Non-Mirror) Variants
variants.note: The cursor moves in a direction rotated by a fixed angle from the hand's movement instead of mirrored. This is the visuomotor rotation paradigm, which could stand as a task of its own.

variants.name: Prism Adaptation Analog
variants.note: The participant wears prism goggles that shift the scene sideways and reaches to targets instead of tracing a shape. This is prism adaptation, which could stand as a task of its own.

variants.name: Dual-Hand Mirror Tracing
variants.note: Both hands trace at once, each with mirror-reversed feedback.

families.rationale: Visuomotor adaptation to mirrored feedback

short_definition: Passive auditory oddball in which rare deviant sounds elicit a negative ERP around 150-250 ms, indexing pre-attentive auditory change detection.
description: Participants are passively exposed to repetitive acoustic stimuli (standard tones, 80%) occasionally interrupted by deviant tones (20%) differing in pitch, duration, or location. The MMN can be elicited without active attention. Recorded via EEG, the MMN appears as a negative deflection peaking at 100-250 ms after deviance onset at frontocentral sites. It reflects automatic, pre-attentive comparison between incoming input and a neural representation of the standard stimulus stored in sensory (echoic) memory. MMN is used as a biomarker of auditory processing capacity and has clinical applications in schizophrenia, coma prognosis, and language development research.

procedure: A repetitive standard tone is occasionally replaced by a deviant tone differing in frequency, duration, or intensity.
Participants typically ignore the sounds while reading or watching a silent video.
manipulations: Deviant type (frequency, duration, intensity, phoneme, location; one or several per stream)
Standard tone sequence (roving vs. fixed standard)
measurements: MMN amplitude and latency (deviant-minus-standard difference wave, peaking 100-250 ms)

material: A repeated standard tone occasionally replaced by a deviant tone differing in pitch, duration, intensity or location.

variants.name: Location/Spatial MMN
variants.note: The deviant comes from a different direction, which may mean loudspeakers instead of headphones.

variants.name: Complex Pattern MMN
variants.note: The regularity is a multi-tone pattern (alternation, rising pair) and the deviant breaks the pattern although every individual tone is familiar.

variants.name: Multi-Feature MMN (Optimum)
variants.note: Several deviant types alternate with the standard in one sequence so that all are collected in one short run.

variants.name: Phoneme/Speech MMN
variants.note: The standard and deviant are speech syllables rather than tones.

variants.name: Visual MMN (vMMN)
variants.note: The ignored stream is visual, shown at the edge of the screen while an unrelated central task occupies the participant.

families.rationale: Passive auditory oddball
