short_definition: Incidental encoding of images followed by a test with old, new, and lure items; discrimination of lures from repetitions indexes pattern separation.
description: The Mnemonic Similarity Task measures hippocampal pattern separation - the ability to distinguish similar but not identical memory representations. During encoding, participants view a series of everyday object images. At test, they classify each image as "old" (previously seen), "similar" (a different exemplar of a studied object with slight visual changes), or "new" (novel). The critical measure is the ability to correctly identify "similar" lures as similar rather than incorrectly endorsing them as old. This discrimination (lure discrimination index) is thought to rely on dentate gyrus/CA3 pattern separation processes and is impaired in early-stage Alzheimer's disease and normal aging.

procedure: Participants study a set of images, then view old items, new items, and similar lures (items resembling studied items).
They classify each as old, new, or similar.
manipulations: Study and test structure (continuous vs. separate phases)
Judged attribute (item location vs. item identity)

material: Pictures of everyday objects, and at test the same objects, new objects and similar lures that differ slightly.

variants.name: Scene MST
variants.note: Indoor and outdoor scenes replace single objects, with lures being slightly altered versions of studied scenes.

variants.name: Continuous MST
variants.note: Study and test are merged into one stream in which each picture is judged old, similar or new as it appears.

variants.name: MST for Faces
variants.note: Faces replace objects, with lures being similar faces or the same face with one feature changed.

variants.name: Spatial MST
variants.note: Objects are studied at screen locations and the test asks whether the location is the same, slightly shifted or new, so what is studied and judged is the item-location pairing rather than the item.

variants.name: Short-Delay vs. Long-Delay MST
variants.note: The test is given immediately in one condition and after hours or a day in another.

families.rationale: Recognition with similar lures

short_definition: Cue predicts potential monetary gain or loss; speeded target response determines outcome. Striatal activity to cues indexes reward anticipation.
description: The Monetary Incentive Delay Task is the dominant paradigm for neuroimaging studies of reward anticipation and consumption. On each trial, a cue signals the potential outcome: reward (gain), loss avoidance, or neutral. After a variable delay period, participants respond to a briefly presented target; successful responses earn the reward (or avoid the loss). The critical contrast is neural activity during the anticipation period (cue-to-target), which robustly activates the ventral striatum/nucleus accumbens, versus the outcome period (after response), which more strongly engages ventromedial prefrontal cortex. The MID has been widely adopted in clinical neuroimaging of addiction, depression, and schizophrenia.

procedure: A cue signals potential reward, loss, or neutral outcome.
After a delay, a target appears and participants make a speeded response.
Outcome depends on response speed.
manipulations: Cue type (reward magnitude, loss magnitude, neutral)
Response effort (grip force or repeated presses vs. single press)
measurements: fMRI activation in ventral striatum (anticipation) and medial PFC (outcome)

material: A cue signalling a possible money gain, a possible loss or nothing, a briefly shown target, and the outcome of the trial.

variants.name: MID with Drug Cues
variants.note: The cues or rewards are pictures of a substance and the task is run with people who use that substance.

variants.name: Passive MID
variants.note: The cue and outcome are shown but the participant presses nothing, with wins and losses following a preset schedule.

variants.name: MID with Effort Component
variants.note: Instead of one quick press the participant must squeeze a hand grip hard enough or press a key many times to earn the cued reward.

families.rationale: Cue announces a potential monetary outcome before a speeded response

short_definition: Repeated execution of a fixed finger sequence; within- and across-session speed and accuracy changes index motor skill learning.
description: Participants are trained to execute finger sequences (e.g., pressing buttons in a specific order: 4-1-3-2-4) either continuously or in discrete blocks. Learning is indexed by decreasing RT, reduced movement duration, and decreased errors. Neuroimaging shows early learning engages cerebellum and prefrontal cortex, while consolidated sequences show greater striatal and reduced cerebellar engagement, reflecting a shift from explicit, attention-demanding processes to implicit, automatic execution. Sleep promotes offline consolidation of motor sequences.

procedure: Participants repeatedly perform a fixed sequence of finger movements (e.g., 4-1-3-2-4) in response to spatial cues.
Over practice, performance speeds up and becomes more automatic.
Optional: After practice the sequence is performed with the other hand, other fingers or mirror-reversed.
manipulations: Movement type (continuous tracking with hidden repeating path)

material: Spatial cues or a digit sequence (such as 4-1-3-2-4) naming the fingers to press in order.

variants.name: Finger Opposition Task
variants.note: The thumb touches the other fingers in a fixed order with no keys or screen; the sequence is given by instruction.

variants.name: Transfer Tests
variants.note: After practice the sequence is performed with the other hand, with other fingers, or mirror-reversed.

variants.name: Continuous Tracking + Sequence
variants.note: The participant follows a moving target with a joystick, and part of the target's path secretly repeats.

families.rationale: Explicit practice of a finger sequence

short_definition: Repeated choice among options with unknown or changing reward distributions; choice sequences dissociate exploration from exploitation.
description: Participants choose among multiple options (the "arms" of a slot machine), each yielding rewards with unknown and often changing probabilities. The central challenge is the explore-exploit dilemma: whether to exploit the currently best-known option or explore alternatives that might yield higher returns. Reward probabilities may be stationary or volatile (drifting over time), with the volatile version (restless bandit) requiring continuous updating of value estimates. This paradigm is the dominant tool in computational psychiatry for studying reinforcement learning, and its computational tractability - fitting with Bayesian, Kalman-filter, or upper-confidence-bound models - has made it central to understanding decision-making deficits in addiction, schizophrenia, depression, and anxiety.

procedure: Participants choose repeatedly among multiple options (arms) that deliver stochastic rewards drawn from different distributions.
They must balance exploring unknown options with exploiting known good ones.
manipulations: Cue before each trial (contextual vs. none)
Effort cost of sampling an option
measurements: Fit to reinforcement learning models (learning rate, inverse temperature)

material: Several options, the arms of a slot machine, each paying out rewards with unknown probabilities that are stationary or drifting.

variants.name: Restless (Volatile) Bandit

variants.name: Contextual Bandit

variants.name: Social Bandit

variants.name: Bandit with Effort Cost
variants.note: Choosing or sampling an option costs key presses or a hard task, so exploration carries an effort cost on top of the usual tradeoff.

short_definition: Participants track a subset of identical moving objects among distractors for several seconds; tracking accuracy indexes sustained multifocal attention.
description: In the Multiple Object Tracking task, participants view a set of identical objects (typically 8-16 circles), a subset of which are briefly designated as targets (by flashing or color). All objects then move independently and randomly for several seconds, and participants must track the targets among distractors. After movement stops, participants identify which objects were the original targets. Performance is measured as tracking accuracy as a function of target load (typically 1-5 targets). The task provides a direct index of how many individual objects can be simultaneously tracked - a measure of visual attention capacity, estimated at approximately 4 objects.

procedure: A set of identical objects (dots) move randomly.
a subset is designated as targets.
After the targets are highlighted, all dots move for several seconds, then participants identify which dots were targets.
manipulations: Added identity report for tracked objects
Grouping of tracked objects (clusters vs. independent)

material: 8-16 identical circles, a few briefly flashed or colored as targets, that then move independently and randomly.

combined_with.note: Gaze is held on the fixation target while the main game is played.

variants.note: Each object carries a hidden identity (letter, picture, or color) and at the end the participant reports which identity is at each target position, so identities bound to tracked positions are studied and recalled to a position cue.

variants.name: 3D MOT (NeuroTracker)
variants.note: The spheres move in a simulated three-dimensional volume seen through a stereoscopic display and a staircase adjusts speed to find the fastest trackable rate.

variants.name: Probe-Based MOT
variants.note: One object is highlighted during or after movement and the participant answers yes or no to whether it is a target, a single old/new judgment instead of selecting all targets.

variants.name: Auditory MOT Analogs
variants.note: The moving items are sounds that move around the listener in virtual auditory space and the target sounds are tracked by ear.

short_definition: Continuous stream in which each item must be compared to the one n items back; accuracy and RT index working memory updating and monitoring.
description: The N-Back task is a continuous performance paradigm in which participants view a sequence of stimuli (letters, numbers, or spatial locations) and judge whether each current stimulus matches the one presented n trials earlier. Difficulty scales parametrically with n (1-back, 2-back, 3-back). The task engages working memory maintenance, updating, and comparison processes. Performance typically shows decreased accuracy and increased RT with higher n values. The N-back is the most widely used working memory paradigm in neuroimaging, consistently activating dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and parietal regions.

procedure: A continuous stream of stimuli is presented.
Participants indicate when the current item matches the one presented N items back.

material: A stream of letters (or numbers or spatial locations), some of which match the item n back.

variants.name: Spatial N-Back
variants.note: A square appears at grid positions and the match is on position n back rather than identity.

variants.name: Emotional N-Back
variants.note: The items are emotional faces or words and the match n back is on identity or on expression.

variants.name: Fractal/Object N-Back
variants.note: The items are unnameable patterns so they cannot be rehearsed verbally.

variants.name: Adaptive N-Back
variants.note: The level n rises or falls between blocks to hold each participant near a target accuracy.

variants.name: Auditory N-Back
variants.note: The items are heard (tones or spoken letters) rather than seen.

families.rationale: Compare each item with the one n back

description: Two streams run at once: a square moving among grid positions and a spoken letter on each trial. The participant responds separately when the position matches n back and when the letter matches n back. It is used mainly in working memory training studies.

short_definition: Hierarchical letters in which large letters are composed of small ones; RT differences between global and local identification index attentional scope.
description: The Navon Task investigates hierarchical processing in vision using compound stimuli - large (global) letters composed of smaller (local) letters (e.g., a large "H" made of small "S" letters). Participants identify either the global or local letter depending on instruction. The robust finding of global precedence shows faster identification of global than local forms, with global-to-local interference exceeding local-to-global interference. The task dissociates dorsal/ventral visual stream contributions and is sensitive to hemispheric specialization (left hemisphere for local, right for global processing).

procedure: A large letter (global) composed of small letters (local) is presented.
Participants identify the letter at the designated level (global or local).
manipulations: Target level (global, local, divided across both)
Congruency (same vs. different letter at two levels)
Level cue (cued per trial vs. fixed per block)
Stimulus type (letters, geometric shapes, emotional faces)
Preceding Navon task and its carry-over to a following task
measurements: Asymmetric interference (global disrupts local more than reverse)

material: Large letters made of small letters (such as an H made of S's), the same or a different letter at the two levels.

variants.name: Mixed/Cued Navon
variants.note: A cue on each trial says which level to report, so the level switches trial by trial instead of being fixed per block.

variants.name: Divided Attention Navon
variants.note: The target may appear at either level, or both levels must be reported, so attention is divided across both levels instead of set to one.

combined_with.note: The target may be at the global or the local level, and both are monitored.

variants.name: Sparse vs. Dense Local Elements
variants.note: The number and spacing of the small letters is varied, which weakens the global advantage when elements are sparse.

variants.name: Emotional Navon
variants.note: The compound figure is a large expressive face built from small expressive faces and the participant reports the emotion at the cued level.

variants.name: Auditory Navon Analogs
variants.note: The hierarchy is a melody built from short note patterns and the participant judges either the contour or the local pattern.

variants.name: Navon Figures with Shapes
variants.note: Geometric shapes replace letters at both levels so reading plays no part.

families.rationale: Global-local interference; could be filed under perceptual judgment

short_definition: Sequence of standards with rare deviants or targets; deviants elicit a large positive ERP around 300 ms (P3a/P3b), indexing attention and context updating.
description: Participants are presented with a stimulus stream containing frequent standard stimuli (80% of trials) and infrequent target (oddball) stimuli (20%) that differ in some dimension (pitch, color, shape). Participants respond (button press) to targets. Target detection elicits the P3b ERP component (300-600 ms, parietal maximum), reflecting stimulus evaluation and working memory updating. Novel or unexpected stimuli also elicit the P3a component (frontocentral), reflecting automatic attention capture. The paradigm is widely used as a biomarker of cognitive function and has clinical applications in ADHD, schizophrenia, and traumatic brain injury.

procedure: A sequence of frequent standard stimuli is occasionally interrupted by rare target (and sometimes novel) stimuli.
Participants count or respond to targets.
manipulations: Response requirement (none vs. count or respond)
measurements: P3b amplitude and latency to targets

material: A stream of frequent standard tones and rare target tones that differ in pitch, sometimes with novel non-target sounds.

variants.name: Three-Stimulus Novelty Oddball
variants.note: Rare, varied novel sounds are added as a third event type that the participant ignores while still responding to the rare target.

variants.name: Visual Oddball
variants.note: The common and rare events are shapes or letters on a screen instead of tones.

variants.name: Passive Oddball
variants.note: No response or count is required and the participant may do something else while the sounds play, so there is no job at all.

variants.name: Active Counting vs. Button-Press Response
variants.note: The participant keeps a silent count of the rare events and reports the total at the end instead of pressing to each one; the standard procedure already allows either.

variants.name: Duration Deviance Oddball
variants.note: The rare tone differs from the common one in duration rather than pitch.

variants.name: Cross-Modal Oddball
variants.note: Common and rare events come in different senses, or the stream mixes senses and the participant responds to rare events in either.

variants.name: Emotional Oddball
variants.note: The rare events are emotional pictures or faces in a stream of neutral ones, shown on a screen.

variants.name: Roving Paradigm
variants.note: A tone repeats and is then replaced by a new tone that becomes the new standard, so any response is to a change from the preceding tone rather than to a fixed rare stimulus; the description does not say whether a response is required.

families.rationale: Rare deviants in a stream of standards

short_definition: Studied items mixed with new lures at test; hit and false-alarm rates yield d' and can be decomposed into recollection and familiarity via ROC or remember/know.
description: Participants study a list of stimuli (words, pictures, or faces) during an encoding phase. In the test phase, they view a mixture of studied (old) and unstudied (new) items and make binary old/new recognition judgments. Performance is analyzed using signal detection measures (hits, false alarms, d') and can be further decomposed into familiarity-based (rapid, automatic) and recollection-based (slower, effortful) processes using confidence ratings or remember/know judgments. Neuroimaging consistently implicates the hippocampus, angular gyrus, and default mode network in successful recognition.

procedure: Participants study a list of items, then view a test list containing studied (old) items and unstudied (new) items and classify each as old or new.
Optional: Items are studied in pairs and the old/new judgment is made on pairs, with rearranged pairs of studied items as lures.
manipulations: Study and test structure (continuous vs. separate lists)

material: A studied list of words (or pictures or faces), and at test the studied items mixed with new ones.

variants.name: Associative Recognition
variants.note: Items are studied in pairs and the old/new judgment is made on pairs, with rearranged pairs of studied items as lures.

variants.name: Forced-Choice Recognition
variants.note: Each test trial shows a studied item beside one or more new items and the participant picks the studied one.

variants.name: Continuous Recognition
variants.note: Study and test are merged into one stream in which every item is judged new or repeated, and an item may repeat again later.

variants.name: DRM (Deese-Roediger-McDermott) False Memory Variant
variants.note: Each study list is built from associates of one unpresented word, and that word is placed among the test items so its false-alarm rate can be measured.

short_definition: Alternating arithmetic verification and word/letter memory items; complex-span score indexes working memory capacity under processing load.
description: The Operation Span Task is a complex span measure of working memory capacity. Participants alternate between a processing task (verifying simple math equations, e.g., "Is (2 x 3) + 1 = 8?") and a memory task (remembering letters or words presented after each equation). After a set of 3-7 equation-letter pairs, participants recall the letters in order. The OSPAN score reflects the ability to maintain memory representations while engaging in concurrent processing - a hallmark of working memory capacity (WMC). OSPAN scores are strong predictors of fluid intelligence, reading comprehension, and general executive function.

procedure: Participants alternate between processing a distractor task (verifying math equations) and remembering items (letters or words).
At the end of each set, they recall items in order.
measurements: Operation span score (items recalled in correct position)
Processing accuracy (to verify engagement with distractor task)

material: Simple math equations to verify (such as (2 x 3) + 1 = 8), each followed by a letter or word to remember.

combined_with.note: An equation is verified between each item to be remembered.

variants.name: Reading Span (RSPAN)
variants.note: The interleaved processing task is judging whether a sentence makes sense instead of verifying an equation, with a word or letter to remember after each sentence.

variants.name: Symmetry Span (SYMSPAN)
variants.note: The processing task is a symmetry judgment and the memoranda are grid positions recalled in order, a spatial version of the same structure.

variants.name: Counting Span
variants.note: The participant counts target shapes in each display and says the total, then recalls the totals in order, so the memoranda are the answers produced by the processing task rather than items presented separately.

variants.name: Shortened OSPAN
variants.note: A named shorter protocol with fewer sets and smaller maximum set sizes that gives similar scores in about half the time.

variants.name: Adaptive OSPAN
variants.note: Set size rises after correct recall and falls after errors so that most trials fall near the participant's limit instead of running a fixed series.

families.rationale: Complex span with interleaved arithmetic

short_definition: Study of cue-target pairs followed by cued recall; proportion recalled indexes associative encoding and retrieval.
description: Participants learn arbitrary associations between stimuli and their locations (or between word pairs). In a typical computerized version (CANTAB PAL), abstract patterns appear in boxes around the screen during the study phase, and during test, patterns are presented centrally and participants must identify the correct box location. Difficulty increases across stages from 1-2 to 6-8 pairs. Performance is measured by patterns correctly learned and errors made. The PAL task is particularly sensitive to hippocampal function and shows early sensitivity to amyloid-beta pathology in preclinical Alzheimer's disease.

procedure: Participants study pairs of items (word-word, face-name, object-location) and are later cued with one member to recall the other.
Optional: The same pairs are studied and tested in alternation several times and accuracy per cycle gives a learning curve.
Optional: A second list re-pairs the same cues with new responses, and memory for the first list after the second, or the second given the first, is tested.

material: Pairs of items - related or unrelated word pairs, face-name pairs, or (in CANTAB PAL) abstract patterns in boxes around the screen.

variants.name: Face-Name Paired Associates
variants.note: Each pair is a face photograph and a name, with the face as cue and the name recalled (or chosen from a list).

variants.name: Object-Location Pairs
variants.note: Each pair is an object and a screen or scene location, with either member able to cue the other.

variants.name: CANTAB PAL
variants.note: A named touchscreen instrument of the object-location form with the number of patterns rising across stages.

variants.name: Cross-Modal Paired Associates
variants.note: The two members of a pair arrive through different senses or formats, such as a sound with a picture.

variants.name: Multi-Trial Learning Curves
variants.note: The same pairs are studied and tested in alternation several times and accuracy per cycle gives a learning curve.

variants.name: Retroactive/Proactive Interference Variants
variants.note: A second list re-pairs the same cues with new responses, and memory for the first list after the second (or the second given the first) is tested.

variants.name: Incidental vs. Intentional Encoding
variants.note: In the incidental condition the participant performs a cover judgment on the pairs (rating fit) and the memory test is a surprise.

families.rationale: Cued recall of studied pairs

short_definition: A neutral CS is paired with an aversive US (shock, loud sound); conditioned responses (SCR, startle, amygdala BOLD) index fear learning.
description: A neutral conditioned stimulus (CS; auditory tone or visual cue) is paired with an aversive unconditioned stimulus (US; mild shock, loud noise). After conditioning, the CS alone elicits conditioned fear responses including skin conductance increases, heart rate changes, freezing (in animals), and subjective fear ratings (in humans). Extinction is measured in a subsequent phase where the CS is presented without the US. The task is fundamental to understanding emotional learning and has been used extensively to study the amygdala's role in fear acquisition and the prefrontal cortex's role in extinction.

procedure: Participants view a neutral stimulus (CS+) paired with an aversive unconditioned stimulus (US, typically mild shock or loud noise).
Another stimulus (CS-) is never paired.
Acquisition is followed by extinction (CS+ presented without US).
Optional: A day or more after extinction the extinguished CS is tested again without the US to measure retention of extinction.
Optional: A single reactivation presentation of the CS a day after acquisition is followed by extinction within a window of minutes to hours.
Optional: After acquisition to one CS, cues differing from it by graded amounts are tested and fear is plotted against similarity.
manipulations: Predictive cue (context as the CS vs. discrete cue)
Number of conditioned cues (compound CS vs. single CS)

material: A neutral visual cue or tone (CS+) paired with a mild shock or loud noise, and a second cue (CS-) that is never paired.

variants.name: Contextual Conditioning
variants.note: No discrete cue predicts the US; it arrives at unpredictable times within one of two settings, so the setting itself becomes the CS.

variants.name: Extinction Recall
variants.note: A day or more after extinction the extinguished CS is tested again without the US to measure retention of extinction.

variants.name: Renewal (Context Change)
variants.note: Acquisition in one setting, extinction in another, and the CS tested back in the original or a new setting where fear returns.

variants.name: Reinstatement
variants.note: After extinction a few unsignalled USs are given and the CS is then tested, where fear returns.

variants.name: Reconsolidation Paradigm
variants.note: A single reactivation presentation of the CS a day after acquisition is followed by extinction within a window of minutes to hours.

variants.name: Generalization Gradient
variants.note: After acquisition to one CS, cues differing from it by graded amounts are tested and fear is plotted against similarity.

variants.name: Instructed vs. Uninstructed
variants.note: Some participants are told in advance which cue predicts the US, so the contingency is given verbally rather than learned by exposure.

variants.name: Compound CS Conditioning
variants.note: Two cues (a light and a tone) are presented together before the US and later tested as elements and as a compound.

families.rationale: CS paired with an aversive US

short_definition: Rhyme judgment, phoneme deletion, or phoneme blending tasks index sensitivity to the sound structure of language.
description: Participants view or hear pairs of words and judge whether they rhyme. The task requires analysis of the sound structure of words, comparison of phonological representations, and a binary decision. Control conditions involve matching for orthographic similarity or judging word identity. fMRI reveals activation in left inferior frontal regions (pars opercularis), left temporoparietal areas, and left superior temporal cortex. The task is widely used in reading research and dyslexia studies, as phonological awareness is a strong predictor of reading ability.

procedure: Participants make explicit judgments about the sound structure of spoken words: rhyme detection, phoneme deletion, phoneme segmentation, or blending.
manipulations: Task type (rhyme, onset, phoneme deletion, blending)
measurements: Correlation with reading ability in developmental populations

material: Spoken words (or nonwords) of varying complexity, judged for rhyme, onset, blending or the sounds left when a phoneme is deleted.

variants.name: Rhyme Oddity
variants.note: Three or four words are heard and the participant picks the one that does not rhyme, instead of judging whether a pair rhymes.

variants.name: Rhyme Production
variants.note: One word is heard and the participant produces words that rhyme with it instead of judging a given pair.

variants.name: Onset Detection
variants.note: The participant names the first sound of a spoken word (or, in a second form, judges whether two words share an onset, which keeps compare); the unit is the onset rather than the rhyme.

variants.name: Phoneme Deletion
variants.note: The participant removes a named sound from a spoken word and says what is left, producing a new item rather than judging one.

variants.name: Phoneme Substitution
variants.note: The participant replaces one sound in a spoken word with another and says the new word; a task type not enumerated in the list.

variants.name: Phoneme Segmentation
variants.note: The participant says each sound of a word separately and in order (in some versions counts them) instead of judging a pair.

variants.name: Blending
variants.note: The sounds of a word are played one at a time and the participant says the word they make, so the input is phonemes and the output a generated word.

variants.name: Spoonerisms
variants.note: Two words are heard and the participant swaps their first sounds and says the result, generating two new words while holding both in mind; a task type not enumerated in the list.

variants.name: Syllable Awareness Tasks
variants.note: The unit is the syllable rather than the phoneme and children count or tap them (the deletion and blending forms would be generate); an easier form for younger children.

families.rationale: Rhyme and phoneme manipulation judgments

short_definition: Naming of pictured objects; RT and errors index lexical retrieval and are sensitive to name agreement, frequency, and age of acquisition.
description: Participants view photographs or line drawings of common objects, animals, or scenes and name each item aloud as quickly and accurately as possible. Naming latency (RT from stimulus onset to vocal response onset) is the primary measure. The task engages multiple stages of language production: conceptual identification, lemma retrieval, phonological encoding, and articulation. fMRI reveals activation in left inferior frontal regions (Broca's area) and temporal cortex. The task is widely used in aphasia research and studies of language production.

procedure: Line drawings or photographs of objects are presented one at a time.
Participants name each object as quickly as possible.
manipulations: Response release (delayed go signal vs. immediate naming)
Naming language (cued per trial; switch vs. repeat)
Retrieval report (know, tip-of-the-tongue, do not know) with partial information
Hint after failed naming (first sound or meaning)

material: Line drawings or photographs of common objects and animals, varying in object frequency, name agreement and visual complexity.

variants.name: Blocked-Cyclic Naming
variants.note: A small picture set is named repeatedly in cycles, in blocks that are all one category or mixed, so that related names compete across trials.

variants.name: Object + Action Naming
variants.note: Pictures of actions are added and the participant names the action with a verb or the object with a noun, in separate or mixed blocks.

variants.name: Bilingual Picture Naming
variants.note: A cue on each trial tells a bilingual participant which language to name the picture in, and trials where the language switches are compared with repeats.

variants.name: Tip-of-the-Tongue (TOT) Paradigm
variants.note: Rarely named items and famous faces provoke states where the name is known but cannot be produced, and the participant reports know / tip-of-the-tongue / do not know plus any partial information, adding a report on their own retrieval state to the naming job.

combined_with.note: When naming fails, the player reports their retrieval state and what they partly know.

variants.name: Naming with Phonological/Semantic Cues
variants.note: When naming fails a hint is given (the first sound, or a description of the meaning), and whether the hint brings out the name is recorded.

families.rationale: Name pictured objects

description: A written or spoken word is presented with each picture, and the participant names the picture while ignoring the word. A word related in meaning (cat for a picture of a dog) slows naming; a word that sounds similar (doll) speeds it.

short_definition: A central or peripheral cue indicates the likely target location; RT differences between valid, neutral, and invalid cues index covert spatial orienting.
description: The Posner Spatial Cueing Task measures covert orienting of visual attention. Participants fixate on a central point with two peripheral locations marked. A cue stimulus appears (exogenous: at the target location; or endogenous: a central arrow) followed by a target stimulus at one of the peripheral locations. Cues can be valid (same location as target) or invalid (opposite location). The cueing effect (faster RT to validly cued targets vs. invalidly cued) reflects the cost and benefit of attentional orienting. The task dissociates different components of attention: engaging, disengaging, and shifting.

procedure: A cue (peripheral flash or central arrow) indicates a likely target location.
The target then appears at the cued or uncued location and participants detect or discriminate it.
measurements: RT difference between valid and invalid trials (attention effect)

material: A central fixation point with two marked peripheral locations, a cue (a peripheral flash or a central arrow), and a target at the cued or the other location.

combined_with.note: Gaze is held on the fixation target while the main game is played.

variants.name: Double-Cue Paradigm
variants.note: Both boxes flash at once, so the cue warns that a target is coming without saying where; the cue becomes an alerting cue.

variants.name: Feature-Based Cueing
variants.note: The cue indicates a feature of the target (color, orientation) rather than its location.

variants.name: Object-Based Cueing
variants.note: Two elongated objects replace the boxes and the cue sits at one end of one object, so the comparison is within versus between objects; the cue and response are unchanged.

variants.name: Cross-Modal Cueing
variants.note: The cue is a sound from one side or a touch on one hand while the target stays visual; only the cue's modality and device change.

variants.name: Detection vs. Discrimination Targets
variants.note: The target job is either a single press for any target, as in the standard form, or a report of which of two target forms appeared.

families.rationale: Canonical spatial cueing paradigm

short_definition: Two-player one-shot or iterated game with cooperate/defect choices and asymmetric payoffs; choice patterns index cooperation and strategic reasoning.
description: The Prisoner's Dilemma is a canonical game theory paradigm for studying cooperation and defection under strategic interdependence. Two players simultaneously choose to cooperate or defect. Mutual cooperation yields moderate rewards for both; mutual defection yields low rewards for both; but if one defects while the other cooperates, the defector receives the highest reward and the cooperator receives nothing (or a penalty). The dominant strategy in single-shot play is to defect, yet human participants frequently cooperate, particularly in iterated versions. The task is central to research on trust, reciprocity, altruism, and the neural substrates of social decision-making.

procedure: Two players simultaneously choose to cooperate or defect.
Payoffs depend on both choices according to a matrix where mutual cooperation beats mutual defection but defection is individually tempting.
manipulations: Number of players and move granularity (public goods contribution)
Punishment option after choices are revealed
Exit option (opt out for a guaranteed small payoff vs. none)

material: A payoff matrix of money amounts for each combination of the two players' choices to cooperate or defect.

variants.name: Sequential PD
variants.note: One player chooses first and the second sees that choice before choosing.

variants.name: Multiplayer/Public Goods Version
variants.note: Several players each contribute an amount to a shared pool that is multiplied and divided equally among all, so there are many players and each chooses an amount rather than simply cooperating or defecting.

variants.note: After the choices are revealed, a player or an observing third party can pay from their own money to reduce a defector's earnings.

variants.note: The other player is a program following a fixed strategy such as always cooperate, always defect or tit-for-tat, and the participant may or may not be told.

variants.note: Before choosing, the participant is shown how often the current partner cooperated in earlier games with other people.

variants.name: Continuous PD
variants.note: Each player chooses how much to cooperate on a scale, for example how much of an endowment to transfer to the partner, rather than making a yes-or-no choice.

variants.note: Each player may opt out for a guaranteed small payoff, and those who play face the usual choice.

short_definition: Learn to choose between stimulus pairs through probabilistic feedback, then select among novel recombinations; choose-A vs. avoid-B accuracy dissociates positive and negative reinforcement learning.
description: The Probabilistic Selection Task, developed by Frank and colleagues, assesses the separable contributions of positive and negative reinforcement learning, linked to striatal Go and NoGo pathway function respectively. During training, participants learn to choose between pairs of stimuli (AB, CD, EF) where each stimulus has a fixed probability of reward (e.g., A=80%, B=20%). At test, stimuli are recombined into novel pairs (e.g., A vs. C, B vs. D). Choosing A in novel contexts indexes Go learning (approach from positive feedback), while avoiding B indexes NoGo learning (avoidance from negative feedback). The task was specifically designed to probe basal ganglia dopaminergic mechanisms and is sensitive to dopaminergic medication effects in Parkinson's disease.

short_definition: Two tasks presented with a short SOA; RT for the second task lengthens as SOA shortens, indexing a central response-selection bottleneck.
description: Two stimuli are presented in rapid succession (S1 then S2, separated by a variable stimulus onset asynchrony or SOA), each requiring its own speeded response (R1 and R2). The robust finding is that R2 is slowed as the SOA decreases - the psychological refractory period effect - because central response-selection processes for S2 must wait until response selection for S1 is complete. Pashler (1994) provided the definitive review establishing the central bottleneck model: perceptual processing and motor execution can overlap between tasks, but response selection (choosing which response to make) represents a serial bottleneck. The PRP paradigm remains the primary tool for mapping the architecture of cognitive processing stages and understanding the limits of multitasking.

procedure: Two stimuli requiring separate speeded responses are presented in rapid succession with a variable stimulus-onset asynchrony (SOA).
Both responses are required.
Optional: Thousands of trials are run across several sessions to see whether the second-response slowing shrinks with practice.

Task compatibility (ideomotor-compatible vs. standard stimulus-response mapping)
Number of tasks (three overlapping tasks vs. two)
measurements: RT2 as a function of SOA (PRP effect: RT2 slowing at short SOAs)
Locus of interference per bottleneck models

short_definition: Simple reaction to visual or auditory stimuli appearing at random intervals over 5-10 minutes; mean RT, lapses, and false starts index sustained attention.
description: The Psychomotor Vigilance Task is a sustained-attention reaction time task widely used in sleep research and fatigue monitoring. Participants monitor a display and respond as quickly as possible to a visual stimulus (typically a millisecond counter) that appears at random inter-stimulus intervals (2-10 seconds) over a 5-10 minute period. The primary measure is the number of lapses (responses >500 ms), reflecting momentary failures of sustained attention. The PVT is considered the gold-standard behavioral measure of vigilance and sleepiness because it is simple, has minimal learning effects, and is highly sensitive to sleep deprivation, circadian misalignment, and time-on-task.

short_definition: Virtual multi-arm maze in which participants retrieve rewards from each arm once; working-memory and reference-memory errors index spatial memory.
description: The Virtual Radial Arm Maze is a spatial memory task adapted from the rodent paradigm. Participants navigate a central platform connected to 8 (or more) radial arms, some of which contain rewards. They must visit all rewarded arms while avoiding revisits (working memory errors) and unbaited arms (reference memory errors). The task dissociates reference memory (knowing which arms are baited across trials) from working memory (remembering which arms have been visited within a trial). Virtual versions rendered on computer screens or in VR maintain the spatial navigation demands while enabling human testing with precise measurement. The task engages hippocampal spatial memory systems and has been used extensively in pharmacological and developmental research.

short_definition: A field of moving dots in which a variable fraction move coherently; direction judgments and RT under varying coherence support drift-diffusion modeling of perceptual decisions.
description: The random dot kinematogram presents a field of moving dots in which a variable proportion move coherently in one direction while the remainder move randomly. Participants judge the direction of coherent motion, and the proportion of coherently moving dots parametrically controls task difficulty. This paradigm is the foundational tool for studying perceptual decision-making and has been central to establishing the neural basis of evidence accumulation, linking single-neuron recordings in area MT/V5 and LIP to drift-diffusion models of choice. It bridges sensory processing and decision-making in a way no other paradigm does as cleanly.

a proportion move coherently in one direction while the rest move randomly.

short_definition: Matrix completion items requiring induction of a rule from a 3x3 array of figures; items correct is a standard measure of non-verbal reasoning.
description: Participants view a matrix pattern with a missing element and select the correct completion from a set of alternatives. The patterns involve systematic variations in features such as shape, size, color, orientation, and number, governed by rules that increase in complexity across test items. Solving each item requires extracting the governing rules and applying them to predict the missing element. Raven's Progressive Matrices is the most widely used culture-reduced measure of fluid intelligence (Gf) and abstract relational reasoning, and is among the most extensively studied psychometric instruments in all of psychology. It has been central to debates about the neural basis of general intelligence, g-loading, and the structure of reasoning.

procedure: Participants view a 3x3 matrix of geometric patterns with one cell missing and select the pattern that completes the matrix from a set of alternatives.
manipulations: Number of relational rules to integrate
Rule types (distribution of values, quantitative progression, figure addition)
Administration format (computerized adaptive vs. fixed item order)
Time limit (strict overall limit vs. untimed)
measurements: Number correct (raw score, often converted to IQ-scale)

material: 3x3 matrices of geometric patterns that vary in shape, size, color, orientation and number, with one cell missing and a set of candidate completions.

short_definition: Choice of the best-matching mental-state word for a photograph of the eye region; accuracy indexes complex emotion and mental-state inference.
description: Participants view photographs showing only the eye and eyebrow region of actors and select which of four mental state descriptors best describes the person's thoughts or feelings. The revised version contains 36 photographs, each with four choices ranging from basic emotions to complex cognitive states (e.g., "sarcastic," "despondent"). The task indexes affective theory of mind and shows deficits in autism spectrum conditions. Performance correlates with amygdala and left inferior frontal gyrus activity.

procedure: Participants view photographs of the eye region of faces and select the mental state (from four word options) that best describes what the person is thinking or feeling.
manipulations: Stimulus format (dynamic video vs. still photograph)

material: Photographs of the eye region of actors' faces, each with four mental-state words ranging from basic emotions to complex states.

short_definition: Classify recognition hits as 'remember' (vivid recollection) or 'know' (familiarity without context); proportions index the relative contributions of recollection and familiarity to recognition memory.
description: During a recognition memory test, participants classify each item they judge as "old" according to the subjective quality of their memory: "remember" if they can recollect specific contextual details from the encoding episode (e.g., what they were thinking, where the item appeared), or "know" if the item feels familiar but retrieval of contextual details fails. Tulving (1985) introduced this distinction to operationalize the difference between episodic recollection and noetic familiarity. The paradigm has become the primary behavioral tool for dual-process theories of recognition memory and has been extensively validated with neuroimaging, revealing dissociable hippocampal (recollection) and perirhinal (familiarity) contributions.

procedure: During a recognition memory test, participants first judge each item as old or new, then classify old responses as 'remember' (vivid recollection of encoding context) or 'know' (familiarity without recollection).
Optional: After the remember or know judgment the participant also answers a source question about the item.
Optional: Items are studied as pairs, and the intact or rearranged judgment and the remember or know judgment are made on the pairing.
measurements: Proportion remember and know responses for hits and false alarms
Estimates of recollection and familiarity (dual-process model parameters)

material: Studied items, typically words (or faces or scenes), mixed at test with new ones.

variants.name: Remember/Know with Source Memory
variants.note: After the remember or know judgment the participant also answers a source question about the item, such as which list or which voice.

variants.name: Associative Remember/Know
variants.note: Items are studied as pairs, and the intact/rearranged judgment and the remember/know judgment are made on the pairing.

families.rationale: Recognition with a remember or know judgment

short_definition: Three cue words linked to a single fourth word; solution rate and solution time index semantic search and insight.
description: The Remote Associates Test measures creative thinking through convergent semantic association. On each trial, participants are given three seemingly unrelated words (e.g., "cottage," "Swiss," "cake") and must find a single word that connects all three (answer: "cheese"). The task requires searching semantic memory broadly, suppressing dominant but incorrect associations, and recognizing the linking concept. RAT performance correlates with measures of creativity, insight problem-solving, and divergent thinking. The task has also been used to study the "Aha!" moment - the subjective experience of sudden insight - and its neural correlates in the right anterior superior temporal gyrus.

procedure: Three seemingly unrelated words are presented (e.g., PINE, CRAB, SAUCE).
Participants find a single word that forms a compound or common phrase with each (APPLE).
manipulations: Item difficulty (associative strength of solution to each cue)
Hint or masked prime before the item
measurements: Solution probability as a function of associative strength

material: Sets of three words (such as cottage, Swiss, cake) that each form a compound or phrase with one solution word, of varying associative strength.

variants.name: Compound RAT (CRAT)
variants.note: Items are restricted to those whose answer forms a compound word or phrase with each cue, rather than being related by meaning alone.

variants.name: Timed vs. Untimed RAT
variants.note: Items are given with no time limit in one arm, sometimes with a break before unsolved items are retried, so the time-limit constraint is removed.

families.rationale: Insight problem solving over words; could be filed under language

short_definition: After initial stimulus-reward learning, the contingencies switch; perseveration and reversal speed index behavioral flexibility.
description: Participants learn a stimulus-outcome association (e.g., stimulus A is rewarded, B is not), then contingencies are reversed. Participants must flexibly adapt their behavior to the new associations. Performance measures include trials to criterion and perseverative errors (continued selection of the previously rewarded stimulus). The task can use deterministic or probabilistic contingencies. Neuroimaging consistently implicates the orbitofrontal cortex and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex in reversal learning, particularly for updating stimulus-outcome associations based on feedback. Some forms take points away for a wrong choice rather than merely withholding a win.

procedure: Participants learn to choose the rewarded stimulus over an unrewarded one.
After reaching criterion, contingencies reverse - the previously correct stimulus becomes incorrect and vice versa.
measurements: Errors to criterion on initial discrimination and on reversals
Perseverative errors (continuing to choose previously correct stimulus)

material: Two stimuli, one rewarded and one not, whose assignment reverses once the participant reaches criterion.

variants.name: Multi-Dimensional Reversal
variants.note: Stimuli differ on several features of which only one predicts reward, and a reversal can switch the rewarded value within that feature or move to a different feature altogether.

variants.name: Reward vs. Punishment Reversal
variants.note: Feedback is win-versus-no-win in some blocks and lose-versus-no-lose in others.

families.rationale: Learned contingencies switch

short_definition: Repeated presentation of a 15-word list with immediate free recall over five trials, an interference list, and delayed recall; indexes verbal learning and forgetting.
description: The RAVLT is a comprehensive measure of verbal episodic memory. A list of 15 unrelated words (List A) is read aloud five times, with free recall tested after each presentation, yielding a learning curve. After the fifth trial, an interference list (List B) is presented once and recalled, followed by immediate recall of List A without re-presentation (retroactive interference). After a 20-30 minute delay, delayed recall and recognition of List A are tested. The RAVLT provides a rich profile of memory processes including acquisition rate, learning plateau, susceptibility to interference, retention over delay, and recognition discrimination.

procedure: A 15-word list (List A) is read aloud five times with free recall after each.
A single interference list (List B) is then read once and recalled.
Immediate and delayed recall of List A follow, plus a recognition test.
Optional: The interference list is learned before the main list instead of after it.
Optional: After each free recall the examiner gives category hints for unrecalled words.

material: A list of 15 unrelated words read aloud (List A), a second interference list (List B), and a recognition list mixing List A words with others.

variants.name: Recognition Trial
variants.note: A yes/no recognition list mixing List A, List B and new words is given after delayed recall.

variants.name: Shortened RAVLT
variants.note: A named short form with fewer learning trials or a shorter list.

variants.name: Proactive Interference Paradigm
variants.note: The interference list is learned before the main list instead of after it, so earlier learning's effect on later recall is measured.

short_definition: Lexical or semantic decision on targets preceded by semantically related or unrelated primes; RT facilitation indexes automatic semantic activation.
description: Word pairs are presented in sequence: a prime word followed by a target. Prime-target relationships are manipulated (semantically related, unrelated, or neutral). Participants typically make lexical decisions on the target. Semantic priming is measured as faster RT to related versus unrelated pairs, reflecting automatic spreading activation through semantic memory networks. SOA manipulation distinguishes automatic (short SOA) from strategic (long SOA) priming.

procedure: A prime word is followed by a target word.
Participants make a lexical decision or naming response to the target.
Prime-target pairs are semantically related or unrelated.
manipulations: SOA (short for automatic priming, long for strategic)
Prime and target type (picture vs. word)
measurements: N400 ERP amplitude reduction for related pairs

material: A prime word followed by a target word or nonword, the pair related by association or category or unrelated.

short_definition: Reading or listening to locally ambiguous sentences; reading-time disruptions and offline comprehension indexes syntactic reanalysis.
description: Participants read sentences containing temporary syntactic ambiguities (garden-path sentences) that initially lead to an incorrect parse before disambiguating information forces reanalysis. Classic example: "The horse raced past the barn fell." Sentences may be presented word-by-word (self-paced reading) or while eye movements are tracked. Comprehension is assessed via subsequent questions. Neuroimaging reveals left inferior frontal and temporal activation during syntactic reanalysis. The task probes how the parser uses syntactic, semantic, and probabilistic cues in real-time language processing.

procedure: Participants read sentences word-by-word or in regions.
Some sentences contain temporary syntactic ambiguities that lead the reader down a wrong parse (garden path) before disambiguation.
manipulations: Ambiguity type (main verb/reduced relative, NP/S, etc.)
Response signal lag after the sentence
measurements: Reading time at disambiguating region (self-paced reading, eye tracking)

material: Written sentences with a temporary syntactic ambiguity (garden-path sentences such as The horse raced past the barn fell), varying in ambiguity type, disambiguation point, plausibility and preceding context.

variants.name: Eye-Tracking Reading
variants.note: The whole sentence is shown at once and gaze is recorded instead of key-press reading times.

variants.name: Speed-Accuracy Tradeoff (SAT) Studies
variants.note: The participant judges each sentence's acceptability at a response signal that comes at one of several delays after the sentence ends.

families.rationale: Read or hear syntactically ambiguous sentences

short_definition: Sequential key-press responses to cued locations; RT speedup on repeating vs random sequences indexes implicit sequence learning.
description: The SRTT measures implicit motor sequence learning. Visual stimuli appear sequentially at different spatial locations, each corresponding to a response button. Participants respond as quickly as possible, unaware that stimuli follow a repeating sequence interspersed with random blocks. Learning is inferred from decreasing RT for the repeating sequence relative to random sequences. The dissociation between improved performance and lack of conscious awareness of the sequence structure is a hallmark of implicit learning and provides evidence for procedural memory systems.

procedure: Stimuli appear at one of several spatial locations in a repeating (but covert) sequence.
Participants respond to each location with a spatially mapped keypress.
Sequence awareness is typically not disclosed.
Optional: After the main task the participant is asked whether a sequence was noticed, asked to reproduce it, or shown fragments to recognize.
measurements: RT slowing when sequence is replaced by random order (sequence learning effect)

material: A stimulus at one of several screen locations, each mapped to a key, following a repeating sequence or a random order.

variants.name: Alternating Serial Reaction Time (ASRT)
variants.note: Fixed-sequence positions alternate item by item with random positions, so the regularity spans every other element.

variants.name: Arm-Reaching/Foot-Stepping SRTT
variants.note: The responses are reaches to targets or steps onto floor pads instead of finger presses.

variants.name: Cross-Modal SRTT
variants.note: The cues are tones of different pitches mapped to keys instead of visual positions, or the modality switches between learning and test.

short_definition: Non-spatial feature (e.g. color) dictates a left/right response while task-irrelevant stimulus location varies; RT cost on incongruent trials indexes spatial response conflict.
description: The Simon Task measures the effect of spatial stimulus-response correspondence on performance. Participants respond to a non-spatial stimulus attribute (e.g., color: press left for red, right for blue) while the stimulus appears on either the left or right side of the screen. When stimulus location corresponds with the assigned response side (congruent), responses are faster and more accurate than when they do not correspond (incongruent). The Simon effect reflects automatic activation of a spatially corresponding response that must be overridden when incongruent. The task is a foundational paradigm for studying stimulus-response compatibility and dimensional overlap.

procedure: Stimuli varying on a non-spatial attribute (color, shape) appear on the left or right.
Participants respond with spatially mapped keys.
On incongruent trials, stimulus location conflicts with response location.
manipulations: Spatial congruency (stimulus side matches or conflicts with response side)
Stimulus and response axis (vertical vs. horizontal)
Accessory tone (same side, opposite side, center)
Prior stimulus-response mapping (reversed training or instruction)
Added flankers around the lateral stimulus
measurements: Delta-plot analysis of time-course of interference

material: Stimuli that differ in color or shape and appear on the left or the right of the screen.

variants.name: Auditory Simon Task
variants.note: A tone in the left or right ear is classified by pitch, so the irrelevant location is the ear of presentation.

variants.name: Simon Task with Accessory Stimuli
variants.note: An irrelevant tone sounds together with the visual stimulus from the same side, the opposite side or the center, acting as an alerting event (simultaneous, not in advance).

variants.name: Joint Simon Task
variants.note: Two people sit side by side, each owning one key and one color, so each performs a go/no-go task while the position conflict reappears.

variants.name: Hybrid Simon-Flanker Task
variants.note: The lateral stimulus is also surrounded by flankers, so its irrelevant location and the neighbouring items both compete with the response on the same trial.

variants.name: Emotional Simon Task
variants.note: Emotional faces or words appear left or right and the response is based on their emotion, or the keys carry positive and negative meanings so emotional content conflicts with the response.

variants.name: Mouse-Tracking Simon
variants.note: The response is a mouse movement to an upper-left or upper-right target and the cursor path is the measure; the trial design is unchanged.

families.rationale: Irrelevant location conflicts with response side

short_definition: MID variant in which cues predict potential social (smiling/frowning face) rather than monetary outcomes; indexes social reward anticipation.
description: The Social Incentive Delay Task is a variant of the Monetary Incentive Delay Task (Task 63) that replaces monetary outcomes with social rewards and punishments. Cues signal the potential for positive social feedback (e.g., a smiling face with a thumbs-up), negative social feedback (e.g., a frowning face with a thumbs-down), or neutral outcomes. Participants then respond to a target stimulus, and outcome delivery depends on response speed. The SID was developed to compare the neural substrates of social versus non-social reward anticipation and consumption, testing whether social rewards engage the same striatal dopaminergic circuitry as monetary rewards. The task has been particularly impactful in autism spectrum disorder research, where reduced social reward sensitivity is hypothesized.

procedure: Cues signal potential social reward (smiling face), social non-reward (neutral face), or control (geometric shape).
After a delay, participants respond to a target.
Outcome is contingent on response speed.
manipulations: Cue type (social reward, social non-reward, non-social control)
Reward type within session (social vs. monetary, cued per trial)
measurements: Comparison of social vs. monetary reward anticipation signals

material: A cue (a smiling face, a neutral face or a geometric shape), a target, and feedback faces such as a smiling face with a thumbs-up or a frowning face with a thumbs-down.

variants.name: SID with Personalized Social Stimuli
variants.note: The reward faces are photographs of people the participant knows rather than strangers.

variants.name: SID vs. MID within-Subjects
variants.note: Social and monetary trials are run in the same session with the cue saying which kind of reward is at stake.

variants.name: SID with Real Social Interaction
variants.note: The social reward is delivered live by an experimenter or confederate over a video link instead of by a stored photograph.

families.rationale: Incentive delay with social outcomes

short_definition: Short memory set followed by a probe; yes/no judgment of set membership. RT typically scales linearly with set size.
description: The Sternberg task measures the speed of short-term memory scanning. On each trial, participants encode a brief study list of 1-6 items, then after a retention interval, judge whether a test probe was in the studied list. The critical finding is that RT increases linearly with memory set size for both positive and negative probes, suggesting serial exhaustive scanning. The slope of the RT-by-set-size function indexes memory scanning speed, while the intercept indexes stimulus encoding and response execution time.

procedure: Participants memorize a small set of items (1-6 digits or letters), then a probe appears and they indicate whether it was in the memory set.
manipulations: Varied vs. fixed set across trials
measurements: RT as a function of set size (slope = scanning rate, ~38 ms/item)

material: A memory set of 1-6 digits or letters followed by a single probe item.

variants.name: Auditory Sternberg
variants.note: The set and the probe are spoken through headphones instead of displayed.

variants.name: Cross-Modal Sternberg
variants.note: The set is presented in one modality and the probe in the other, so the match is made on identity rather than on the item's look or sound.

variants.name: Sternberg with Irrelevant Items
variants.note: Some set items are cued as not to be remembered, or extra items are shown during the delay, and some probes match these, so one or both of the study instruction and the interval filler change.

variants.name: Recent-Probes Sternberg
variants.note: Some negative probes were members of the previous trial's set, so rejecting them is slower; a negative-probe subtype rather than a change in structure.

families.rationale: Memory set followed by a membership probe

short_definition: Choice RT task in which an occasional stop signal requires response cancellation; stop-signal reaction time (SSRT) estimates inhibitory latency.
description: The Stop-Signal Task measures the ability to inhibit a prepotent motor response after it has been initiated. Participants perform a primary go task (button press to go signals) but on a subset of trials, a stop signal (auditory tone or visual cue) appears after a variable delay (stop-signal delay, SSD), instructing them to cancel their response. SSD is adjusted dynamically using a staircase procedure converging on 50% inhibition probability. The key measure is stop-signal reaction time (SSRT), estimated using the race model framework, which indexes the latency of the internal inhibitory process.

procedure: On most trials, participants make a speeded response to a go stimulus.
On a minority of trials, a stop signal (tone or visual cue) appears after the go stimulus, instructing them to withhold their response.
manipulations: Response on signal trials (change to a different response vs. cancel)
Stop-signal relevance (every signal vs. only signals or responses of one kind)
Context cue paired with stop probability (background color)
measurements: Stop-signal reaction time (SSRT, estimated via race model)
Probability of stopping at each SSD

material: A go stimulus on every trial and, on a minority of trials, a stop signal (a tone or a visual cue) after a variable delay.

variants.name: Fixed SSD Procedure
variants.note: The stop signal comes at a few preset delays instead of a delay adjusted to the participant's performance.

variants.name: Stop-Change Task
variants.note: On signal trials the planned response is cancelled and a different one made instead, a response demand the vocabulary lacks (cancel and replace rather than cancel).

variants.name: Proactive vs. Reactive Inhibition Manipulation
variants.note: A cue or block instruction announces how likely a stop signal is on coming trials, the same demand-probability cue proposed for Cued Go/No-Go.

variants.name: Stop-Signal in Reaching/Saccade Tasks
variants.note: The response to be cancelled is an arm reach or a saccade rather than a key press; only effector and recording change.

variants.name: Context-Dependent Stop-Signal
variants.note: A display feature such as background color is paired with a stop probability, and the participant learns the pairing rather than being told it.

families.rationale: Cancel an initiated response on a stop signal

short_definition: Naming the ink color of color words while ignoring word meaning; RT and error costs on incongruent trials index selective attention and conflict control.
description: The Stroop Color-Word Task is a classic measure of selective attention and cognitive control that requires participants to identify the ink color of printed words while ignoring the semantic content. In the standard version, participants view color names (e.g., "RED," "BLUE") printed in incongruent ink colors and must respond with the ink color rather than reading the word. The task measures reaction time and accuracy across congruent trials (word and color match), incongruent trials (word and color conflict), and neutral trials. Performance reflects the ability to overcome automatic word-reading processes and requires engagement of executive control mechanisms. The Stroop interference effect (slowed RT on incongruent trials) is one of the most robust findings in cognitive psychology.

procedure: Color words (RED, BLUE) are printed in incongruent ink colors.
Participants name the ink color while ignoring the word.
manipulations: Task rule (name the ink color, read the word, count the words)
Trial sequence (ignored word becomes next trial's ink color)

material: Color words (RED, BLUE) printed in ink of a matching or a different color.

variants.name: Manual (Button-Press) Stroop
variants.note: The ink color is reported by key press, one key per color, instead of aloud.

variants.name: Counting Stroop
variants.note: A number word is printed one to four times and the participant reports how many words there are while ignoring the number named.

variants.name: Spatial Stroop
variants.note: A direction word or arrow appears at a screen position and the participant reports its position while ignoring its meaning; some versions instead report the meaning while ignoring the position.

variants.name: Numerical Stroop
variants.note: Two digits of different physical sizes are shown and the participant picks the numerically larger (ignoring size) or physically larger (ignoring value), a comparison between two simultaneous items.

variants.name: Face-Word Stroop
variants.note: An emotion word is written across an expressive face and the participant names the expression while ignoring the word.

variants.name: Color-Shape Stroop
variants.note: Objects with a strongly associated color are shown in the wrong color and the participant names the displayed color while the known color interferes.

variants.name: Priming Stroop
variants.note: Each item is preceded by a prime that is neutral, matches or conflicts with it, giving advance feature information that may be valid or invalid.

families.rationale: Canonical interference task

short_definition: Speeded responses to frequent non-targets with withholding on rare targets; commission errors and RT variability index sustained attention lapses.
description: The Sustained Attention to Response Task is a Go/No-Go variant specifically designed to measure sustained attention failures and mind-wandering. Participants respond (button press) to every digit presented (1-9) except for one designated target digit (typically "3"), to which they must withhold their response. Digits are presented at a fixed rate (e.g., every 1150 ms), and the high frequency of Go responses (89%) creates a monotonous, routinized response pattern that promotes attentional lapses. Errors of commission (responding to the No-Go target) serve as the primary index of attention failure. The SART has become the standard behavioral measure for studying mind-wandering, task-unrelated thought, and attentional lapses.

procedure: Single digits (1-9) are presented one at a time.
Participants respond to every digit except a designated target (typically 3).
The high go-probability induces a prepotent response tendency.
manipulations: Added thought probes during the task
Stimulus type (shapes, colors or oriented lines vs. digits)
Response rule (switching during the run vs. fixed)
Number of withhold items (multiple targets vs. one)
measurements: Commission errors (responses to the no-go target)

material: Single digits 1-9 shown one at a time at a fixed rate, one of them (typically 3) the no-go target.

variants.name: SART with Thought Probes
variants.note: At unpredictable points the stream pauses and the participant reports what they were just thinking, inserting a self-report into the ongoing task.

combined_with.note: A thought probe interrupts the stream.

variants.name: Perceptual SART
variants.note: Shapes, colors or oriented lines replace the digits, with one of them as the withhold item.

variants.name: Sustained Attention Task with Response Switching
variants.note: The key-press rule changes periodically during the run, so the participant tracks the current rule while still withholding on the rare item.

variants.name: Sustained Attention with Clock Task
variants.note: A clock hand advances in regular jumps and the participant presses only when it double-jumps, a continuous detection task with a rare target rather than a go/no-go stream (this is the Mackworth Clock, arguably a different task listed as a variation).

variants.name: Child-Adapted SART
variants.note: Pictures of animals or objects replace the digits and the pace is slowed for children.

families.rationale: Go/no-go structure with rare withhold targets; also a vigilance measure
Thought probes inserted in the stream sample mind wandering

short_definition: Alternation between two or more simple tasks on cue; switch-cost RT and errors index task-set reconfiguration.
description: Task Switching paradigms measure cognitive flexibility by requiring participants to alternate between two or more classification tasks. Participants view stimuli (e.g., bivalent alphanumeric characters like "G3") and perform different classifications depending on a task cue (letter: vowel/consonant; digit: odd/even). Tasks alternate in predictable sequences (e.g., AABB) or are cued on each trial. The primary measures are switch costs (increased RT and errors when switching tasks vs. repeating the same task) and mixing costs (increased RT in mixed-task blocks vs. single-task blocks). Switch costs reflect the time for task-set reconfiguration.

procedure: Participants alternate between two (or more) simple tasks on the same stimuli, cued by an explicit cue or a predictable alternation schedule.
manipulations: Task sequence (random cued, predictable alternating runs, voluntary choice)
Added conflict from an irrelevant stimulus dimension
measurements: Switch cost (switch - repeat RT and accuracy)
Preparation effect (switch cost reduction with longer CSI)

material: Bivalent characters such as a letter-digit pair (G3), classified by the letter (vowel or consonant) or the digit (odd or even) as the cue directs.

variants.name: Alternating Runs (AABB)
variants.note: No cue is given; the task changes on a fixed, known schedule (two trials of each), often marked by the stimulus stepping around a grid, and the participant must keep track.

variants.name: Voluntary Task Switching
variants.note: The participant chooses which task to do on each trial, with no cue, and is asked to use both about equally often and in a random order.

variants.name: Mixing Cost Paradigm
variants.note: Pure blocks in which the rule never changes are added and compared with the mixed blocks of the standard form.

variants.name: Univalent vs. Bivalent Stimuli
variants.note: Stimuli that afford only one of the rules (letters only, digits only) are compared with the standard bivalent stimuli that afford both, which removes the previous rule as a competitor in the univalent condition.

variants.name: Predictable vs. Random Task Sequences
variants.note: A fixed, known order of tasks with no cue is compared with the standard random, cued order.

variants.name: Task Switching with Conflict
variants.note: The stimuli are built as Stroop or flanker items, so an irrelevant dimension competes with the response as well as the previous task's rule.

families.rationale: Alternate between tasks on cue

short_definition: Cue words are presented with instructions to either retrieve or suppress their learned associate; later memory for suppressed items indexes retrieval-induced forgetting through inhibition.
description: Participants first learn cue-target word pairs (e.g., "ordeal-roach"). In the critical phase, cues are presented and participants are instructed either to recall the target (Think) or to prevent the target from coming to mind (No-Think). On a final test, suppressed (No-Think) items show reduced recall relative to baseline items that were learned but not presented during the critical phase. Anderson and Green (2001) introduced this paradigm as a memory analog of the Go/No-Go motor inhibition task, arguing that just as people can stop a motor action, they can suppress retrieval of unwanted memories. The paradigm has become central to research on memory suppression, PTSD, and the role of prefrontal control over hippocampal memory retrieval.

procedure: Participants learn cue-target word pairs to criterion.
In the critical phase, cues are presented and participants either actively recall the target (think) or suppress retrieval (no-think).
A final test probes all pairs.
manipulations: Think vs. no-think vs. baseline (not presented in critical phase)
Independent probe test (IP: novel cue for same target)
Intrusion report after each no-think trial
Suppression strategy (thought substitution vs. direct blocking)
measurements: IP test (demonstrates inhibitory vs. associative interference account)

material: Cue-target word pairs (such as ordeal-roach) whose cues are later shown alone with an instruction to recall the target or keep it from mind.

variants.name: TNT with Intrusion Reporting
variants.note: After each no-think trial the participant reports whether the partner word came to mind anyway.

variants.name: Emotional TNT
variants.note: The suppressed material is negative or trauma-related (unpleasant words, or faces paired with disturbing scenes) and is compared with neutral material.

families.rationale: Retrieve or suppress an associate on cue

short_definition: Rearrange colored beads on pegs to match a goal state in the minimum number of moves; pre-execution latency and move efficiency index planning.
description: The Tower of London Task is a planning and problem-solving task. Participants are presented with two configurations of colored beads on pegs: a start state and a goal state. They must plan and execute a sequence of moves to transform the start state into the goal state in the minimum number of moves, following movement constraints (one bead at a time, peg capacity limits). Problem difficulty is manipulated by the minimum number of moves required (2-7). Performance is measured by moves to solution, planning time, and accuracy. The task is a key measure of prefrontal executive function, particularly planning and look-ahead.

procedure: Three pegs hold colored discs in a start configuration.
Participants move discs one at a time to reach a goal configuration in the minimum number of moves.
measurements: Number of problems solved in minimum moves

material: Colored beads on three pegs, in a start configuration and a goal configuration.

variants.note: The balls and pegs are shown on a screen and moved by mouse rather than being handled; the problem itself is unchanged.
